I had been eating some hay, and the wind rolled a little lock of it that way, and the poor creature put out her long thin neck and picked it up, and then turned and looked about for more. There was a hopeless look in the dull eye that I could not help noticing, and then, as I was thinking where I had seen that horse before, she looked full at me and said, “Black Beauty, is that you?”

It was Ginger! but how changed! The beautifully arched and glossy neck was now straight, and lank, and fallen in; the clean straight legs and delicate fetlocks were swelled; the joints were grown out of shape with hard work; the face, that was once so full of spirit and life, was now full of suffering, and I could tell by the heaving of her sides, and her frequent cough, how bad her breath was.
Our drivers were standing together a little way off, so I sidled up to her a step or two, that we might have a little quiet talk. It was a sad tale that she had to tell.

After a twelvemonth's run off at Earlshall, she was considered to be fit for work again, and was sold to a gentleman. For a little while she got on very well, but after a longer gallop than usual the old strain returned, and after being rested and doctored she was again sold. In this way she changed hands several times, but always getting lower down.

“And so at last,” said she, “I was bought by a man who keeps a number of cabs and horses, and lets them out. You look well off, and I am glad of it, but I could not tell you what my life has been. When they found out my weakness they said I was not worth what they gave for me, and that I must go into one of the low cabs, and just be used up; that is what they are doing, whipping and working with never one thought of what I suffer--they paid for me, and must get it out of me, they say. The man who hires me now pays a deal of money to the owner every day, and so he has to get it out of me too; and so it's all the week round and round, with never a Sunday rest.”
I said, “You used to stand up for yourself if you were ill-used.”

“Ah!” she said, “I did once, but it's no use; men are strongest, and if they are cruel and have no feeling, there is nothing that we can do, but just bear it--bear it on and on to the end. I wish the end was come, I wish I was dead. I have seen dead horses, and I am sure they do not suffer pain; I wish I may drop down dead at my work, and not be sent off to the knackers.”
I was very much troubled, and I put my nose up to hers, but I could say nothing to comfort her. I think she was pleased to see me, for she said, “You are the only friend I ever had.”
Just then her driver came up, and with a tug at her mouth backed her out of the line and drove off, leaving me very sad indeed.

A short time after this a cart with a dead horse in it passed our cab-stand. The head hung out of the cart-tail, the lifeless tongue was slowly dropping with blood; and the sunken eyes! but I can't speak of them, the sight was too dreadful. It was a chestnut horse with a long, thin neck. I saw a white streak down the forehead. I believe it was Ginger; I hoped it was, for then her troubles would be over. Oh! if men were more merciful they would shoot us before we came to such misery.
translated_paragraphs: 有一天，我们和许多出租马车一起，等在一座正演奏音乐的公园外。一辆破马车驶到我们身旁。拉车的是匹栗色老马，毛没人理，骨头根根凸着，前膝向前弯曲，两条前腿直打颤。我正在吃干草，一阵风把一小撮草卷到那边。这可怜的马伸长细脖子叼起草来，又转头找还有没有。她那暗淡的眼睛里有一种绝望的神气，我怎么也没法不留意。正想着我以前在哪里见过她，她直直地看着我说：“黑骏马，是你吗？”
是姜儿！她的模样怎么变成了这样！从前那道漂亮的、泛着光的颈弧，如今细瘦塌陷，直梗梗的。原先笔直的腿和秀气的球节都肿了，沉重的工作使关节变了形。那张从前生机勃勃的脸上如今全是痛苦。她的肋腹一起一伏，频频咳嗽。我看得出，她连喘口气都很费力。
我们的车夫站在稍远处聊天。我往她身边挪了一两步，好安安静静说会儿话。她要告诉我的，是个伤心的故事。
她在厄尔庄园放养休息了一年，人们便觉得她又能干活了，把她卖给一位先生。开头一阵还不错，一次奔跑比平常长了些，旧伤又犯了。休养，治伤，再卖掉。她就这样换过几回主人，一回比一回差。
“到后来，”她说，“一个有好多出租马车和马的人买了我。看起来你过得好，我真高兴。我过的那些日子，哪里说得清。他们发现我有病，就说我不值他们花的钱，得去拉最次的车，一直用到不能用为止。他们当真这样干，用鞭子抽着我干活，从没想过我疼不疼。他们说买我花了钱，就得从我身上挣回来。现在租我用的那个人，每天得付给东家好大一笔，他也得从我身上挣回来。于是我一周绕着一周跑，连星期日都歇不了。”
我说：“从前别人待你不好，你会反抗的呀。”
“唉，那时候是啊。可没用。人比我们有力气。他们要是冷酷起来，什么也不体恤，我们能做的只剩忍着，一直忍到头。我巴不得到头了，巴不得已经死了。我见过死马，我敢说它们不再觉得疼。我只盼能拉着车一下子倒下去，别把我送到屠马场。”
我难过极了，把鼻子贴到她的鼻子上，没有一句能安慰她的话。我想她见到我是高兴的，因为她说：“你是我这辈子有过的唯一的朋友。”
她的车夫恰好过来，猛一扯她嘴里的嚼子，叫她倒退出队伍，赶车走了。剩我独自伤心。
没过多久，一辆载着死马的大车从我们的候客处驶过。马头悬在车尾外，没了生气的舌头缓缓滴着血。还有那双凹陷的眼睛！可我讲不下去了，那景象太可怕。这匹马是栗色的，脖子又细又长。我看见额头上有一道白痕。我觉得那是姜儿。我盼着是姜儿，那样她的苦就吃完了。唉，人要是再仁慈一点，就该趁我们还没落到这步田地，先开一枪，让我们免受这样的苦。

sections.title_zh: 第三部 / 第41章　肉贩
source_paragraphs: I saw a great deal of trouble among the horses in London, and much of it might have been prevented by a little common sense. We horses do not mind hard work if we are treated reasonably, and I am sure there are many driven by quite poor men who have a happier life than I had when I used to go in the Countess of W----'s carriage, with my silver-mounted harness and high feeding.

It often went to my heart to see how the little ponies were used, straining along with heavy loads or staggering under heavy blows from some low, cruel boy. Once I saw a little gray pony with a thick mane and a pretty head, and so much like Merrylegs that if I had not been in harness I should have neighed to him. He was doing his best to pull a heavy cart, while a strong rough boy was cutting him under the belly with his whip and chucking cruelly at his little mouth. Could it be Merrylegs? It was just like him; but then Mr. Blomefield was never to sell him, and I think he would not do it; but this might have been quite as good a little fellow, and had as happy a place when he was young.

I often noticed the great speed at which butchers' horses were made to go, though I did not know why it was so till one day when we had to wait some time in St. John's Wood. There was a butcher's shop next door, and as we were standing a butcher's cart came dashing up at a great pace. The horse was hot and much exhausted; he hung his head down, while his heaving sides and trembling legs showed how hard he had been driven. The lad jumped out of the cart and was getting the basket when the master came out of the shop much displeased. After looking at the horse he turned angrily to the lad.

“How many times shall I tell you not to drive in this way? You ruined the last horse and broke his wind, and you are going to ruin this in the same way. If you were not my own son I would dismiss you on the spot; it is a disgrace to have a horse brought to the shop in a condition like that; you are liable to be taken up by the police for such driving, and if you are you need not look to me for bail, for I have spoken to you till I'm tired; you must look out for yourself.”

During this speech the boy had stood by, sullen and dogged, but when his father ceased he broke out angrily. It wasn't his fault, and he wouldn't take the blame; he was only going by orders all the time.

“You always say, 'Now be quick; now look sharp!' and when I go to the houses one wants a leg of mutton for an early dinner and I must be back with it in a quarter of an hour; another cook has forgotten to order the beef; I must go and fetch it and be back in no time, or the mistress will scold; and the housekeeper says they have company coming unexpectedly and must have some chops sent up directly; and the lady at No. 4, in the Crescent, never orders her dinner till the meat comes in for lunch, and it's nothing but hurry, hurry, all the time. If the gentry would think of what they want, and order their meat the day before, there need not be this blow up!”

“I wish to goodness they would,” said the butcher; “'twould save me a wonderful deal of harass, and I could suit my customers much better if I knew beforehand--But there! what's the use of talking--who ever thinks of a butcher's convenience or a butcher's horse! Now, then, take him in and look to him well; mind, he does not go out again to-day, and if anything else is wanted you must carry it yourself in the basket.” With that he went in, and the horse was led away.

But all boys are not cruel. I have seen some as fond of their pony or donkey as if it had been a favorite dog, and the little creatures have worked away as cheerfully and willingly for their young drivers as I work for Jerry. It may be hard work sometimes, but a friend's hand and voice make it easy.

There was a young coster-boy who came up our street with greens and potatoes; he had an old pony, not very handsome, but the cheerfullest and pluckiest little thing I ever saw, and to see how fond those two were of each other was a treat. The pony followed his master like a dog, and when he got into his cart would trot off without a whip or a word, and rattle down the street as merrily as if he had come out of the queen's stables. Jerry liked the boy, and called him “Prince Charlie”, for he said he would make a king of drivers some day.

There was an old man, too, who used to come up our street with a little coal cart; he wore a coal-heaver's hat, and looked rough and black. He and his old horse used to plod together along the street, like two good partners who understood each other; the horse would stop of his own accord at the doors where they took coal of him; he used to keep one ear bent toward his master. The old man's cry could be heard up the street long before he came near. I never knew what he said, but the children called him “Old Ba-a-ar Hoo”, for it sounded like that. Polly took her coal of him, and was very friendly, and Jerry said it was a comfort to think how happy an old horse might be in a poor place.
translated_paragraphs: 在伦敦，我见过无数匹马遭罪。很多苦处，原本只需要一点常识就可避免。我们马并不怕干重活，只要人待我们合情合理。我敢说，有些赶车人虽然穷，他们的马过的日子，却比从前我替W伯爵夫人拉车、披着镶银马具、吃着精饲料时快活得多。

看见那些矮种小马受到怎样的对待，我常常心疼。有的拼尽全力拖着重重的载荷，有的在某个粗野、残忍的小子狠揍之下踉踉跄跄。有一回我看见一匹灰色矮马，鬃毛浓密，脑袋漂亮，长得那么像快腿儿，若不是正在套车干活，我一定会朝他嘶鸣招呼。他拼着命拖一辆沉重的大车，一个粗壮蛮横的男孩却在拿鞭子抽打他肚子底下，又凶狠地扯他那张小嘴。会不会是快腿儿呢？模样简直一样。可布洛姆菲尔德先生答应过永不把他卖掉，我也相信他不会卖。这匹马说不定也是个一样好的小家伙，年轻时也有过一样快活的家。
我常留意到，肉贩的马总被赶得飞快。以前我不明白为什么，直到一天我们在圣约翰伍德区等了好一阵，才听出点缘故。隔壁就是一家肉铺。我们正站着，一辆送肉的车疾驰而来。马浑身发烫，疲惫不堪，头垂着，肋间剧烈起伏，四腿颤抖。一望便知道刚才给人赶得多狠。小伙计跳下车子，正要提篮子，他的主人已很不高兴地从店里走出来。他看看那匹马，气冲冲地转向小伙计。
“我要跟你说多少回，别这样赶马？上一匹就是给你毁了的，连它的呼吸都留下了病根。现在你打算用同样的法子再毁一匹。你要不是我亲儿子，我立刻就把你解雇。把马弄成这副模样带回店里，可耻！你这样赶车，警察很可能抓你。真给抓了，别指望我去给你交保。该说的我说得已经厌了，你自己看着办吧。”
父亲说这番话时，男孩阴着脸，倔强地站在一旁。等父亲一住口，他便气呼呼地嚷开来。不是他的错，他不肯背这个罪名。他从头到尾都不过是照人家吩咐办事。

“你总说，‘快点，快点！手脚麻利些！’我挨家一跑，这一户临时要一条羊腿做早午饭，非叫我一刻钟内送回来不可。那一户的厨子先前忘了订牛肉，非叫我马上取去、马上赶回，否则她家夫人要骂。又一位管家说有客人突然登门，得立刻送几块带骨肉排来。还有新月街四号那位太太，总要等午餐的肉已经上门，她才肯订晚餐的。这一天到晚，除了赶，赶，赶，还是什么？要是那些有身份的人肯先想想自己要什么，头一天就订好肉，咱们哪用得着大吵这一顿！”
“老天知道我巴不得他们肯！”肉贩说，“那样我能少操多少心呀。要是事先知道，我给客人备的肉也能更合他们心意。可算了，说了有什么用？有谁会想想肉贩方不方便，又有谁会想想肉贩的马？好啦，带它进去，悉心照料。记住，今天不能再叫它出门。有人还要什么，你自己提篮子送去。”说完，他进了店，那匹马也给牵走了。
可也并非每个男孩都残忍。我见过有的男孩爱惜自家的小马或驴子，就像疼爱一条最宠爱的狗。那些小家伙替年轻的车夫干活，也跟我替杰里干活一样，干得快活又情愿。事情有时确实辛苦，可朋友的一只手、一个声音，就能叫艰难的活轻松起来。
有个摆卖水果蔬菜的小伙子，常常赶车到我们街上卖青菜和土豆。他有一匹老矮马，样子谈不上漂亮，却是我见过最开朗、最有劲的小家伙之一。看他俩彼此那样亲爱，真是享受。小马像狗一样跟着主人。男孩一上车，无需鞭子，不劳一句话，它就自己小跑开去，拉着车在街上辘辘地跑得那样快活，像是刚从女王的御马厩里出来。杰里喜欢那个孩子，管他叫“查理王子”，因为他觉得，那孩子将来会当上车夫中的国王。

还有位老人，常拉着小煤车到我们街上来。他戴顶搬煤工的帽子，外表粗陋，身上乌黑。他和他的老马常常在街上并肩缓步，像两个合得来、知根底的老搭档。哪几家从他这里买煤，小马自会在门前停脚，还总有一只耳朵侧向主人。老人还离得老远，叫卖声就传遍全街。他到底喊什么，我从没听明白。孩子们管他叫“老巴——呼”，因为听上去就像这么个声响。波莉家的煤都向他买，待他也很亲热。杰里说，想到老马即使住在穷地方，也能活得这样快活，心里便觉得宽慰。

sections.title_zh: 第三部 / 第42章　选举
source_paragraphs: As we came into the yard one afternoon Polly came out. “Jerry! I've had Mr. B---- here asking about your vote, and he wants to hire your cab for the election; he will call for an answer.”

“Well, Polly, you may say that my cab will be otherwise engaged. I should not like to have it pasted over with their great bills, and as to making Jack and Captain race about to the public-houses to bring up half-drunken voters, why, I think 'twould be an insult to the horses. No, I shan't do it.”
“I suppose you'll vote for the gentleman? He said he was of your politics.”
“So he is in some things, but I shall not vote for him, Polly; you know what his trade is?”
“Yes.”

“Well, a man who gets rich by that trade may be all very well in some ways, but he is blind as to what workingmen want; I could not in my conscience send him up to make the laws. I dare say they'll be angry, but every man must do what he thinks to be the best for his country.”
On the morning before the election, Jerry was putting me into the shafts, when Dolly came into the yard sobbing and crying, with her little blue frock and white pinafore spattered all over with mud.
“Why, Dolly, what is the matter?”
“Those naughty boys,” she sobbed, “have thrown the dirt all over me, and called me a little raga--raga--”

“They called her a little 'blue' ragamuffin, father,” said Harry, who ran in looking very angry; “but I have given it to them; they won't insult my sister again. I have given them a thrashing they will remember; a set of cowardly, rascally 'orange' blackguards.”
Jerry kissed the child and said, “Run in to mother, my pet, and tell her I think you had better stay at home to-day and help her.”
Then turning gravely to Harry:

“My boy, I hope you will always defend your sister, and give anybody who insults her a good thrashing--that is as it should be; but mind, I won't have any election blackguarding on my premises. There are as many 'blue' blackguards as there are 'orange', and as many white as there are purple, or any other color, and I won't have any of my family mixed up with it. Even women and children are ready to quarrel for the sake of a color, and not one in ten of them knows what it is about.”
“Why, father, I thought blue was for Liberty.”

“My boy, Liberty does not come from colors, they only show party, and all the liberty you can get out of them is, liberty to get drunk at other people's expense, liberty to ride to the poll in a dirty old cab, liberty to abuse any one that does not wear your color, and to shout yourself hoarse at what you only half-understand--that's your liberty!”
“Oh, father, you are laughing.”

“No, Harry, I am serious, and I am ashamed to see how men go on who ought to know better. An election is a very serious thing; at least it ought to be, and every man ought to vote according to his conscience, and let his neighbor do the same.”
translated_paragraphs: 一天下午，我们进院时，波莉走出来说：“杰里！B先生才来过，打听你这一票要投给谁，还想租你这辆车选举那天用。他过些时会来听回话。”
“好吧，波莉，”杰里说，“你只管说，我的车那天另有用处。车身上要糊满他们那些大海报，我可不乐意。至于要杰克和上尉四处飞跑，一站站赶到酒馆，去接送那些半醉的选民，我看对马也是一种侮辱。不，我不会接这趟活。”
“我想你的票会投给那位先生吧？他说你跟他的政见一样。”
“有些事看法一样。不过我的票不会投给他，波莉。你知道他是靠哪一行吃饭的吧？”
“知道。”
“嗯，靠那一行发了财的人，某些方面可能也挺好，不过劳动人家需要什么，他却看不见。凭我的良心，我不能把他送上去制定法律。他们说不定要生气，可一个人得想想怎样才对自己的国家最好，就照那样做。”
选举前一天的早晨，杰里正把我牵进车杠间，多莉抽抽搭搭哭着走进院子，小蓝裙和白围裙从上到下溅满了泥。
“哎呀，多莉，怎么了？”
“那些坏男孩，”她抽泣着说，“拿泥巴往我身上扔，还骂我是小破……小破……”
“他们骂她是‘蓝派的小破落户’，爸爸，”哈里也跑了进来，很生气的样子，“可我已经收拾过他们。他们不会再欺负我妹妹了。我给了他们一顿好打，他们忘不了的。这群没胆子的流氓，‘橙派’的坏坯子！”
杰里亲亲孩子，说：“小宝贝，快进屋找妈妈，告诉她，我看你今天最好待在家里，帮帮她。”
随后，他神色认真地转向哈里，说：
“好孩子，我希望你一直护着妹妹。谁侮辱她，就给谁一顿教训，这才像话。可你听着，在我这里，不许拿选举那套脏话来骂人。‘蓝派’的坏蛋不比‘橙派’少，白色、紫色，或是别的什么颜色，也各有一样多的坏蛋。我不许咱们家里任何一个人掺进这种事。如今连女人和孩子都准备为一种颜色吵架，可十个人里有一个清楚自己到底在吵什么，就不错了。”
“可是爸爸，我原以为蓝色代表自由。”
“孩子，自由不是从颜色里来的。颜色只表明你属于哪一派。你能从颜色里得到的全部自由，就是可以花别人的钱把自己喝醉，可以坐一辆又旧又脏的出租马车去投票，可以开口辱骂一切不佩戴你这一派颜色的人，还可以为自己一知半解的事情把喉咙都喊哑。这就是你说的自由！”
“哎，爸爸，您这是逗我笑吧。”
“不，哈里，我是认真的。看见一群本该更懂事的人竟然闹成那样，我都为他们害臊。选举是一桩十分严肃的事，至少它理应严肃。每个人都该凭自己的良心投票，也容许邻人这样做。”

sections.title_zh: 第三部 / 第43章　患难时的朋友
sections.title_en: Part III / 43 A Friend in Need
source_paragraphs: The election day came at last; there was no lack of work for Jerry and me. First came a stout puffy gentleman with a carpet bag; he wanted to go to the Bishopsgate station; then we were called by a party who wished to be taken to the Regent's Park; and next we were wanted in a side street where a timid, anxious old lady was waiting to be taken to the bank; there we had to stop to take her back again, and just as we had set her down a red-faced gentleman, with a handful of papers, came running up out of breath, and before Jerry could get down he had opened the door, popped himself in, and called out, “Bow Street Police Station, quick!” so off we went with him, and when after another turn or two we came back, there was no other cab on the stand. Jerry put on my nose-bag, for as he said, “We must eat when we can on such days as these; so munch away, Jack, and make the best of your time, old boy.”

I found I had a good feed of crushed oats wetted up with a little bran; this would be a treat any day, but very refreshing then. Jerry was so thoughtful and kind--what horse would not do his best for such a master? Then he took out one of Polly's meat pies, and standing near me, he began to eat it. The streets were very full, and the cabs, with the candidates' colors on them, were dashing about through the crowd as if life and limb were of no consequence; we saw two people knocked down that day, and one was a woman. The horses were having a bad time of it, poor things! but the voters inside thought nothing of that; many of them were half-drunk, hurrahing out of the cab windows if their own party came by. It was the first election I had seen, and I don't want to be in another, though I have heard things are better now.

Jerry and I had not eaten many mouthfuls before a poor young woman, carrying a heavy child, came along the street. She was looking this way and that way, and seemed quite bewildered. Presently she made her way up to Jerry and asked if he could tell her the way to St. Thomas' Hospital, and how far it was to get there. She had come from the country that morning, she said, in a market cart; she did not know about the election, and was quite a stranger in London. She had got an order for the hospital for her little boy. The child was crying with a feeble, pining cry.

“Poor little fellow!” she said, “he suffers a deal of pain; he is four years old and can't walk any more than a baby; but the doctor said if I could get him into the hospital he might get well; pray, sir, how far is it; and which way is it?”
“Why, missis,” said Jerry, “you can't get there walking through crowds like this! why, it is three miles away, and that child is heavy.”
“Yes, bless him, he is; but I am strong, thank God, and if I knew the way I think I should get on somehow; please tell me the way.”

“You can't do it,” said Jerry, “you might be knocked down and the child be run over. Now look here, just get into this cab, and I'll drive you safe to the hospital. Don't you see the rain is coming on?”
“No, sir, no; I can't do that, thank you, I have only just money enough to get back with. Please tell me the way.”

“Look you here, missis,” said Jerry, “I've got a wife and dear children at home, and I know a father's feelings; now get you into that cab, and I'll take you there for nothing. I'd be ashamed of myself to let a woman and a sick child run a risk like that.”
“Heaven bless you!” said the woman, and burst into tears.
“There, there, cheer up, my dear, I'll soon take you there; come, let me put you inside.”
As Jerry went to open the door two men, with colors in their hats and buttonholes, ran up calling out, “Cab!”

“Engaged,” cried Jerry; but one of the men, pushing past the woman, sprang into the cab, followed by the other. Jerry looked as stern as a policeman. “This cab is already engaged, gentlemen, by that lady.”
“Lady!” said one of them; “oh! she can wait; our business is very important, besides we were in first, it is our right, and we shall stay in.”

A droll smile came over Jerry's face as he shut the door upon them. “All right, gentlemen, pray stay in as long as it suits you; I can wait while you rest yourselves.” And turning his back upon them he walked up to the young woman, who was standing near me. “They'll soon be gone,” he said, laughing; “don't trouble yourself, my dear.”

And they soon were gone, for when they understood Jerry's dodge they got out, calling him all sorts of bad names and blustering about his number and getting a summons. After this little stoppage we were soon on our way to the hospital, going as much as possible through by-streets. Jerry rung the great bell and helped the young woman out.
“Thank you a thousand times,” she said; “I could never have got here alone.”
“You're kindly welcome, and I hope the dear child will soon be better.”

He watched her go in at the door, and gently he said to himself, “Inasmuch as ye have done it to one of the least of these.” Then he patted my neck, which was always his way when anything pleased him.

The rain was now coming down fast, and just as we were leaving the hospital the door opened again, and the porter called out, “Cab!” We stopped, and a lady came down the steps. Jerry seemed to know her at once; she put back her veil and said, “Barker! Jeremiah Barker, is it you? I am very glad to find you here; you are just the friend I want, for it is very difficult to get a cab in this part of London to-day.”
“I shall be proud to serve you, ma'am; I am right glad I happened to be here. Where may I take you to, ma'am?”
“To the Paddington Station, and then if we are in good time, as I think we shall be, you shall tell me all about Mary and the children.”
We got to the station in good time, and being under shelter the lady stood a good while talking to Jerry. I found she had been Polly's mistress, and after many inquiries about her she said:
“How do you find the cab work suit you in winter? I know Mary was rather anxious about you last year.”

“Yes, ma'am, she was; I had a bad cough that followed me up quite into the warm weather, and when I am kept out late she does worry herself a good deal. You see, ma'am, it is all hours and all weathers, and that does try a man's constitution; but I am getting on pretty well, and I should feel quite lost if I had not horses to look after. I was brought up to it, and I am afraid I should not do so well at anything else.”

“Well, Barker,” she said, “it would be a great pity that you should seriously risk your health in this work, not only for your own but for Mary's and the children's sake; there are many places where good drivers or good grooms are wanted, and if ever you think you ought to give up this cab work let me know.”
Then sending some kind messages to Mary she put something into his hand, saying, “There is five shillings each for the two children; Mary will know how to spend it.”
Jerry thanked her and seemed much pleased, and turning out of the station we at last reached home, and I, at least, was tired.
translated_paragraphs: 选举日终于来了，我和杰里一点不缺活干。先来一位胖乎乎、脸庞浮肿的绅士，拎着毯布旅行袋，要去主教门车站。随后一行人叫我们送他们去摄政公园。接下来，另一条支路有位胆小而忧心的老太太，等着上银行。到了那里，我们还须候着送她回来。才放她下车，就有一位红脸膛的先生，手里攥着一把文书，跑得上气不接下气。杰里还没来得及从座位上下来，他已经自己拉开车门，钻了进去，喊道：“弓街警察局，快！”我们便送了他去。又转过一两趟，等回到候客处，那里连另一辆车也没了。杰里给我套上挂在鼻口前的饲料袋。照他的话，“碰上这种日子，什么时候能吃，什么时候就得吃。嚼吧，杰克，老伙计，抓紧这一点工夫。”

我发现袋里是分量很足的压碎燕麦，用一点麸皮拌润了。换了哪天这也算好吃的，在那时尤其叫我恢复精神。杰里做事这样细心，待我这样好，哪匹马肯不为这样的主人尽力呢？他也从车里取出一个波莉做的肉馅饼，站在我身边吃起来。街上挤得很，披着各位候选人代表色的出租马车在人群中冲来撞去，仿佛别人的手脚和性命都无所谓。那天我们看见两个人被撞倒，其中一个是位妇人。那些马可苦了！但车里的选民全不放在心上。好多乘客已半醉，遇上同党的人经过，就从车窗里欢呼。这是我见过的第一场选举，我可不想再被卷进第二场。虽说我听人讲，如今比先前好些了。
杰里和我还没吃下几口，就有一位贫穷的年轻母亲沿街走来，怀里抱着个不轻的孩子。她东张西望，显得十分茫然。不久她走到杰里面前，问他能不能指一指去圣托马斯医院的路，还要走多远。她说自己是今天早上搭赶集的车从乡下来，不知道要办选举，在伦敦也完全不认得路。她为小儿子拿到一张入院凭单。那孩子在哭，声音微弱而凄苦。
“可怜的小家伙！”她说，“他很痛。他四岁了，却跟婴儿一样不能走路。医生说，只要我能把他送进医院，也许就能治好。先生，请问还有多远？我该往哪边走？”
“哎，太太，”杰里说，“叫你抱着他穿过这么挤的人群，那怎么走得到？路足有三英里，孩子又这样沉。”
“是啊，愿上帝保佑他，是够沉的。可是我有力气，感谢上帝。要是知道路，我想总会有办法走过去。请您指给我吧。”
“不行，”杰里说，“你会叫人撞倒，孩子可能被车轧着。听我的，坐进这辆马车吧，我稳稳当当送你到医院去。没看见就要下雨了吗？”
“不，先生，不行。谢谢您，我不能坐车。我口袋里刚够回去的路费。请您只告诉我往哪儿走。”
“太太，你听我说，”杰里说，“我家里有妻子，有心爱的孩子，我知道做父亲的是怎样一副心肠。现在你上车，我免费送你去。若是让一个女人抱着生病的孩子去冒这种险，我会为自己害臊。”
“愿上天保佑您！”女人说完，眼泪一下涌了出来。
“好了，好了，好太太，别难过，我一会儿就送你到。来，让我帮你坐进去。”
杰里刚走去开门，就有两个男人跑上来，帽子和衣服扣眼都别着党派的彩带，嘴里直叫：“马车！”
“有人订了！”杰里喊。可其中一人已从女人身旁挤过，一跃而入，另一个也跟了进去。杰里板起脸来，像一位警察那么严肃。“两位先生，先前订了这辆车的，就是这位女士。”
“女士！”其中一个说，“噢，她可以等！我们的事很要紧。再说我们先坐进来，我们有这个权利，也不打算出去。”
杰里脸上掠过一抹滑稽的微笑。他把车门关好，说：“很好，两位先生，愿意待多久请便。二位在里面歇着，我等得起。”他背转身，走向站在我身边的年轻母亲，笑着说：“他们马上会走的。好太太，别为这事着急。”
他们果然很快就走了。明白了杰里使的是什么招数以后，两人下了车，冲他骂尽所有难听的话，虚张声势地嚷着要记下他的车号，要给他发传票。这一点耽搁过去，我们很快向医院出发，尽量拣支路走。杰里拉响医院的大门铃，扶那个年轻女人下车。
“谢谢您一千次，”她说，“我一个人无论如何也来不到这里。”
“很乐意为你效劳，希望可爱的孩子能快快好起来。”
他一直目送她进了门，然后轻轻自言自语：“这些事，你们既做在一个最小的人身上……”他随即又拍拍我的脖子，只要碰到什么使他欣慰的事情，他一贯都会这么做。
雨这时下得急了。我们正要离开医院，大门又打开，门房朝外喊：“马车！”我们停下，一位女士从台阶上走下来。杰里好像一眼认出了她。她掀开面纱，说：“巴克！杰里迈亚·巴克，是你吗？很高兴在这里见到你。我正需你这样的朋友帮忙，今天在伦敦这一带可真难叫到车。”
“能替夫人效劳，是我的荣幸。这也赶得真巧，我很高兴。请问夫人，您要我送您到哪里？”
“去帕丁顿车站。如果到得早，我想会赶得及的，你就把玛丽和孩子们的近况都讲给我听。”
我们到车站时还早。那里能遮风挡雨，女士便站着同杰里聊了好一阵。我听出来，她是波莉从前的女主人。她问过波莉的许多细事之后，又说：
“冬天拉出租马车，你身子吃得消吗？我知道去年玛丽曾经颇为你担心。”
“是的，夫人，她是担心了。上回我咳嗽很厉害，一路咳到天暖。有时工作得在外面等到很晚，她真会十分忧心。您知道，夫人，这活时辰没定，天气也不管好坏，对人的身体确实是个考验。不过现在我还过得不错。要是身边没马照看，我反倒会茫然得不知怎么办。我从小就在这一行长大，怕是做别的都做不了这么好。”
“嗯，巴克，”她说，“要让这份活真正伤了身子，实在可惜。不单为你自己，也为了玛丽和孩子们。有不少地方需要好的车夫，或是好的马夫。今后哪一天若觉得该把出租马车这份活放下了，一定让我知道。”
随后，她托杰里代向玛丽亲切问好，又往他手里放下一点东西，说：“两个孩子，每人五先令。玛丽知道该怎么用。”
杰里谢过她，模样十分高兴。我们拐出车站，最后总算到了家。至于我，反正我是累了。

sections.title_zh: 第三部 / 第44章　老上尉和它的接替者
sections.title_en: Part III / 44 Old Captain and His Successor
source_paragraphs: Captain and I were great friends. He was a noble old fellow, and he was very good company. I never thought that he would have to leave his home and go down the hill; but his turn came, and this was how it happened. I was not there, but I heard all about it.

He and Jerry had taken a party to the great railway station over London Bridge, and were coming back, somewhere between the bridge and the monument, when Jerry saw a brewer's empty dray coming along, drawn by two powerful horses. The drayman was lashing his horses with his heavy whip; the dray was light, and they started off at a furious rate; the man had no control over them, and the street was full of traffic.

One young girl was knocked down and run over, and the next moment they dashed up against our cab; both the wheels were torn off and the cab was thrown over. Captain was dragged down, the shafts splintered, and one of them ran into his side. Jerry, too, was thrown, but was only bruised; nobody could tell how he escaped; he always said 'twas a miracle. When poor Captain was got up he was found to be very much cut and knocked about. Jerry led him home gently, and a sad sight it was to see the blood soaking into his white coat and dropping from his side and shoulder. The drayman was proved to be very drunk, and was fined, and the brewer had to pay damages to our master; but there was no one to pay damages to poor Captain.

The farrier and Jerry did the best they could to ease his pain and make him comfortable. The fly had to be mended, and for several days I did not go out, and Jerry earned nothing. The first time we went to the stand after the accident the governor came up to hear how Captain was.

“He'll never get over it,” said Jerry, “at least not for my work, so the farrier said this morning. He says he may do for carting, and that sort of work. It has put me out very much. Carting, indeed! I've seen what horses come to at that work round London. I only wish all the drunkards could be put in a lunatic asylum instead of being allowed to run foul of sober people. If they would break their own bones, and smash their own carts, and lame their own horses, that would be their own affair, and we might let them alone, but it seems to me that the innocent always suffer; and then they talk about compensation! You can't make compensation; there's all the trouble, and vexation, and loss of time, besides losing a good horse that's like an old friend--it's nonsense talking of compensation! If there's one devil that I should like to see in the bottomless pit more than another, it's the drink devil.”
“I say, Jerry,” said the governor, “you are treading pretty hard on my toes, you know; I'm not so good as you are, more shame to me; I wish I was.”
“Well,” said Jerry, “why don't you cut with it, governor? You are too good a man to be the slave of such a thing.”
“I'm a great fool, Jerry, but I tried once for two days, and I thought I should have died; how did you do?”

“I had hard work at it for several weeks; you see I never did get drunk, but I found that I was not my own master, and that when the craving came on it was hard work to say 'no'. I saw that one of us must knock under, the drink devil or Jerry Barker, and I said that it should not be Jerry Barker, God helping me; but it was a struggle, and I wanted all the help I could get, for till I tried to break the habit I did not know how strong it was; but then Polly took such pains that I should have good food, and when the craving came on I used to get a cup of coffee, or some peppermint, or read a bit in my book, and that was a help to me; sometimes I had to say over and over to myself, 'Give up the drink or lose your soul! Give up the drink or break Polly's heart!' But thanks be to God, and my dear wife, my chains were broken, and now for ten years I have not tasted a drop, and never wish for it.”
“I've a great mind to try at it,” said Grant, “for 'tis a poor thing not to be one's own master.”

“Do, governor, do, you'll never repent it, and what a help it would be to some of the poor fellows in our rank if they saw you do without it. I know there's two or three would like to keep out of that tavern if they could.”

At first Captain seemed to do well, but he was a very old horse, and it was only his wonderful constitution, and Jerry's care, that had kept him up at the cab work so long; now he broke down very much. The farrier said he might mend up enough to sell for a few pounds, but Jerry said, no! a few pounds got by selling a good old servant into hard work and misery would canker all the rest of his money, and he thought the kindest thing he could do for the fine old fellow would be to put a sure bullet through his head, and then he would never suffer more; for he did not know where to find a kind master for the rest of his days.
The day after this was decided Harry took me to the forge for some new shoes; when I returned Captain was gone. I and the family all felt it very much.

Jerry had now to look out for another horse, and he soon heard of one through an acquaintance who was under-groom in a nobleman's stables. He was a valuable young horse, but he had run away, smashed into another carriage, flung his lordship out, and so cut and blemished himself that he was no longer fit for a gentleman's stables, and the coachman had orders to look round, and sell him as well as he could.
“I can do with high spirits,” said Jerry, “if a horse is not vicious or hard-mouthed.”

“There is not a bit of vice in him,” said the man; “his mouth is very tender, and I think myself that was the cause of the accident; you see he had just been clipped, and the weather was bad, and he had not had exercise enough, and when he did go out he was as full of spring as a balloon. Our governor (the coachman, I mean) had him harnessed in as tight and strong as he could, with the martingale, and the check-rein, a very sharp curb, and the reins put in at the bottom bar. It is my belief that it made the horse mad, being tender in the mouth and so full of spirit.”
“Likely enough; I'll come and see him,” said Jerry.

The next day Hotspur, that was his name, came home; he was a fine brown horse, without a white hair in him, as tall as Captain, with a very handsome head, and only five years old. I gave him a friendly greeting by way of good fellowship, but did not ask him any questions. The first night he was very restless. Instead of lying down, he kept jerking his halter rope up and down through the ring, and knocking the block about against the manger till I could not sleep. However, the next day, after five or six hours in the cab, he came in quiet and sensible. Jerry patted and talked to him a good deal, and very soon they understood each other, and Jerry said that with an easy bit and plenty of work he would be as gentle as a lamb; and that it was an ill wind that blew nobody good, for if his lordship had lost a hundred-guinea favorite, the cabman had gained a good horse with all his strength in him.

Hotspur thought it a great come-down to be a cab-horse, and was disgusted at standing in the rank, but he confessed to me at the end of the week that an easy mouth and a free head made up for a great deal, and after all, the work was not so degrading as having one's head and tail fastened to each other at the saddle. In fact, he settled in well, and Jerry liked him very much.
translated_paragraphs: 上尉和我是很好的朋友。他是个高尚的老伙计，跟他做伴很愉快。我从没想过，他也会有一天得离开这个家，走下坡路。可终于轮到了他，事情是这样发生的。我没亲自在场，经过却听得很全。
那天，他和杰里载了几位客人，送往伦敦桥那边的大火车站。回来时，大约在桥与纪念碑之间，杰里看见一辆啤酒厂的空板车迎面而来，由两匹力气很大的马拉着。赶车人正拿沉重的鞭子抽马，车上又是空的，马便以吓人的速度往前猛冲。那人已制不住它们，而街上到处是往来的车辆。

一个年轻姑娘给撞倒，车从她身上轧过。下一刻，那两匹马就冲撞在我们的出租马车上。两个车轮都被扯了下来，车子倾覆在地。上尉也被拖倒，车杠断裂，其中一根戳进他的身体侧面。杰里也被摔了出去，好在仅仅撞得青肿。没人能说清他是怎样脱险的，他自己一直说那是神迹。等可怜的上尉被扶起来，人们才发现他浑身都是严重的割伤、撞伤。杰里轻轻牵着他回家，血浸透一身白毛，从他的身体一侧和肩头往下滴。那情景叫人心痛。酒厂车夫被证实当时酩酊大醉，罚了款，酒厂老板也得赔偿我主人的损失。可怜的上尉，却没有谁能给他赔偿。
马医和杰里尽力缓解他的疼痛，叫他躺得舒服一些。我们的客车非修不可，接连好几天我没出过门，杰里一文钱也挣不到。事故以后第一次重新来到候客处，头儿便走近，打听上尉的情形。

“他好不了了，”杰里说，“至少再也干不了我这行的活。马医今早就是这么说的。他说也许还能拉货车之类。这可叫我难受坏了。拉货车！我见过在伦敦周围拉货车的马最后落到什么地步。我只盼望那些醉鬼全都收进疯人院去，别让他们在街上横冲直撞，撞上清醒的人。他们若只管摔断自己的骨头，砸烂自己的货车，弄瘸自己的马，那是他们自己的事，我们还可以不管。可我看，受苦的怎么总是无辜者？随后他们还谈什么赔偿！哪能赔偿得来？那么多烦恼、苦闷、白白耽搁的时光不说，还要失去一匹像老朋友一样的好马。讲什么赔偿，都是废话！若说哪一个魔鬼最叫我巴不得它坠进无底深渊，那就是酒魔。”
“我说，杰里，”头儿说，“你这几句可踩痛了我的脚趾头。你知道，我没有你那么好，是我该害臊。我要是能像你就好了。”
“那你为什么不跟酒来个一刀两断，头儿？”杰里说，“你是这么好的人，何必做这种东西的奴隶。”
“杰里，我是个大糊涂蛋。可有一回我试了两天，觉得自己快要死了。你是怎么办到的？”

“我也好几个星期过得十分艰难。你要知道，我从没喝醉过，可我发现自己已经做不了自己的主人。酒瘾一上来，要说声‘不’，真得下很大力气。我明白，两者之中，一个必须认输，要么酒魔，要么我杰里·巴克。我就对自己说，上帝若肯助我，败的不会是杰里·巴克。可那是场硬仗，我需要一切得得到的帮助，因为在真正要打破这个习惯以前，根本没料到它能有那么大的力气。波莉那时尽心帮我，让我总有好吃的食物。瘾头发作，我就来杯咖啡，或吃点薄荷，或读一会儿自己的小书，这几样都帮得上忙。有时还得反反复复对自己说：‘放下酒，否则就丢了灵魂！放下酒，否则就要伤透波莉的心！’感谢上帝，也感谢我亲爱的妻子。我的锁链终于断了。这十年来我滴酒未沾，连喝酒的念头也没再有过。”
“我真有心试着走一走这条路，”格兰特说，“做不了自己的主人，这滋味可不好。”
“试试吧，头儿，一定试试。你永远不会后悔。站上那些苦命的弟兄，看见你不用酒也过得去，那对他们也是多大的帮助！我知道至少有两三个，要是有办法，他们也很想不再走进那家酒馆。”

上尉起初看着还好，但他毕竟是匹很老的马。这么久还能拉出租马车，全靠他天生体格出色，也靠杰里照料。如今身子已经大大地垮了。马医说，也许能将养到值几英镑，再卖掉。杰里说，不成！把一个忠实的老伙伴卖去受苦、做重活，那样得来的几英镑，会把他手里的其余每一文钱都蚀坏。他觉得，能为这个漂亮老伙计做的最仁慈的事，是稳稳当当送一颗子弹进它的脑袋。那样它再也不会受苦。因为他实在不知道到哪里才能找个好主人，肯收留它走完最后的岁月。
作出这个决定以后，第二天哈里带我到铁匠铺换新掌。我回来时，上尉已经不在了。这件事，我和家里人人都十分难受。
杰里现在需要再找一匹马。很快就从一位相识那里听到了消息，那人在一位贵族的马厩里当副马夫。他们有一匹年轻有价值的好马，先前却曾受惊狂奔，撞上一辆马车，把爵爷摔出去，又给自己弄得满身伤疤，已经不够体面，不能留在绅士的马厩里。车夫领了命，要出门找找买家，能卖多好便卖多好。
“我和精神特别旺盛的马处得来，”杰里说，“只要它没学坏，嘴也没变硬。”
“它身上一丁点恶习都没有，”那人说，“嘴也娇嫩得很。要我说，那场意外也正是由此来的。它刚剪过毛，天气坏，活动又远远不够。一旦有机会出门，浑身活力饱胀得像个大气球。我们的头儿，就是车夫，把它往车上套的时候，可着劲地勒紧、扣牢。有把马头往下牵制的限头带，有吊缰，又上了极利的杠杆衔铁，缰绳还扣在最底端的横杆上。我相信那是把它逼疯了。它的嘴那么娇嫩，性子又是这么烈。”
“很可能是这么回事。我去看看它。”杰里说。

次日，烈性子就来到家里。烈性子是它的名字。那是一匹漂亮的棕马，身上一根白毛也没有，个子跟上尉一样高，一颗脑袋长得十分英俊，年纪只有五岁。我为了表示同伴的情谊，友好地同他打过招呼，却没向他盘问什么。第一夜他非常不安，不肯卧下，只管上下拉扯穿过铁环的笼头绳，把绳端的坠块搡来撞去，咚咚打在饲料槽上，弄得我睡不着。不过第二天，拉了五六个钟头出租马车，再回来，他已经安定，也懂事得多。杰里常拍拍他，跟他说许多话，没多久他们就心有默契了。杰里说，用一道合适、不难受的衔铁，给够他事情做，他会像小羊一样温顺。又说，再坏的风也总会给谁吹来一点好处。那位爵爷虽失去一匹值一百基尼的宠儿，他这车夫倒得到一匹满身力气的好马。
烈性子本以为沦为出租马车的马，是身份大大地跌落，又十分讨厌站在候客的队伍里。可到周末，他私下对我承认，只要嘴里舒服，脑袋自由自在，这些好处就足够补偿许多缺憾。况且说到底，这份活儿，也没把脑袋和尾巴都拴到鞍子上、两头扯在一起那样丢尊严。他逐渐安顿得很好，杰里很喜欢他。

sections.title_zh: 第三部 / 第45章　杰里的新年
source_paragraphs: For some people Christmas and the New Year are very merry times; but for cabmen and cabmen's horses it is no holiday, though it may be a harvest. There are so many parties, balls, and places of amusement open that the work is hard and often late. Sometimes driver and horse have to wait for hours in the rain or frost, shivering with the cold, while the merry people within are dancing away to the music. I wonder if the beautiful ladies ever think of the weary cabman waiting on his box, and his patient beast standing, till his legs get stiff with cold.

I had now most of the evening work, as I was well accustomed to standing, and Jerry was also more afraid of Hotspur taking cold. We had a great deal of late work in the Christmas week, and Jerry's cough was bad; but however late we were, Polly sat up for him, and came out with a lantern to meet him, looking anxious and troubled.

On the evening of the New Year we had to take two gentlemen to a house in one of the West End Squares. We set them down at nine o'clock, and were told to come again at eleven, “but,” said one, “as it is a card party, you may have to wait a few minutes, but don't be late.”
As the clock struck eleven we were at the door, for Jerry was always punctual. The clock chimed the quarters, one, two, three, and then struck twelve, but the door did not open.

The wind had been very changeable, with squalls of rain during the day, but now it came on sharp, driving sleet, which seemed to come all the way round; it was very cold, and there was no shelter. Jerry got off his box and came and pulled one of my cloths a little more over my neck; then he took a turn or two up and down, stamping his feet; then he began to beat his arms, but that set him off coughing; so he opened the cab door and sat at the bottom with his feet on the pavement, and was a little sheltered. Still the clock chimed the quarters, and no one came. At half-past twelve he rang the bell and asked the servant if he would be wanted that night.
“Oh, yes, you'll be wanted safe enough,” said the man; “you must not go, it will soon be over,” and again Jerry sat down, but his voice was so hoarse I could hardly hear him.

At a quarter past one the door opened, and the two gentlemen came out; they got into the cab without a word, and told Jerry where to drive, that was nearly two miles. My legs were numb with cold, and I thought I should have stumbled. When the men got out they never said they were sorry to have kept us waiting so long, but were angry at the charge; however, as Jerry never charged more than was his due, so he never took less, and they had to pay for the two hours and a quarter waiting; but it was hard-earned money to Jerry.
At last we got home; he could hardly speak, and his cough was dreadful. Polly asked no questions, but opened the door and held the lantern for him.
“Can't I do something?” she said.
“Yes; get Jack something warm, and then boil me some gruel.”

This was said in a hoarse whisper; he could hardly get his breath, but he gave me a rub-down as usual, and even went up into the hayloft for an extra bundle of straw for my bed. Polly brought me a warm mash that made me comfortable, and then they locked the door.

It was late the next morning before any one came, and then it was only Harry. He cleaned us and fed us, and swept out the stalls, then he put the straw back again as if it was Sunday. He was very still, and neither whistled nor sang. At noon he came again and gave us our food and water; this time Dolly came with him; she was crying, and I could gather from what they said that Jerry was dangerously ill, and the doctor said it was a bad case. So two days passed, and there was great trouble indoors. We only saw Harry, and sometimes Dolly. I think she came for company, for Polly was always with Jerry, and he had to be kept very quiet.
On the third day, while Harry was in the stable, a tap came at the door, and Governor Grant came in.
“I wouldn't go to the house, my boy,” he said, “but I want to know how your father is.”
“He is very bad,” said Harry, “he can't be much worse; they call it 'bronchitis'; the doctor thinks it will turn one way or another to-night.”
“That's bad, very bad,” said Grant, shaking his head; “I know two men who died of that last week; it takes 'em off in no time; but while there's life there's hope, so you must keep up your spirits.”

“Yes,” said Harry quickly, “and the doctor said that father had a better chance than most men, because he didn't drink. He said yesterday the fever was so high that if father had been a drinking man it would have burned him up like a piece of paper; but I believe he thinks he will get over it; don't you think he will, Mr. Grant?”
The governor looked puzzled.
“If there's any rule that good men should get over these things, I'm sure he will, my boy; he's the best man I know. I'll look in early to-morrow.”
Early next morning he was there.
“Well?” said he.
“Father is better,” said Harry. “Mother hopes he will get over it.”

“Thank God!” said the governor, “and now you must keep him warm, and keep his mind easy, and that brings me to the horses; you see Jack will be all the better for the rest of a week or two in a warm stable, and you can easily take him a turn up and down the street to stretch his legs; but this young one, if he does not get work, he will soon be all up on end, as you may say, and will be rather too much for you; and when he does go out there'll be an accident.”
“It is like that now,” said Harry. “I have kept him short of corn, but he's so full of spirit I don't know what to do with him.”

“Just so,” said Grant. “Now look here, will you tell your mother that if she is agreeable I will come for him every day till something is arranged, and take him for a good spell of work, and whatever he earns, I'll bring your mother half of it, and that will help with the horses' feed. Your father is in a good club, I know, but that won't keep the horses, and they'll be eating their heads off all this time; I'll come at noon and hear what she says,” and without waiting for Harry's thanks he was gone.
At noon I think he went and saw Polly, for he and Harry came to the stable together, harnessed Hotspur, and took him out.

For a week or more he came for Hotspur, and when Harry thanked him or said anything about his kindness, he laughed it off, saying it was all good luck for him, for his horses were wanting a little rest which they would not otherwise have had.

Jerry grew better steadily, but the doctor said that he must never go back to the cab work again if he wished to be an old man. The children had many consultations together about what father and mother would do, and how they could help to earn money.
One afternoon Hotspur was brought in very wet and dirty.
“The streets are nothing but slush,” said the governor; “it will give you a good warming, my boy, to get him clean and dry.”
“All right, governor,” said Harry, “I shall not leave him till he is; you know I have been trained by my father.”
“I wish all the boys had been trained like you,” said the governor.
While Harry was sponging off the mud from Hotspur's body and legs Dolly came in, looking very full of something.
“Who lives at Fairstowe, Harry? Mother has got a letter from Fairstowe; she seemed so glad, and ran upstairs to father with it.”
“Don't you know? Why, it is the name of Mrs. Fowler's place--mother's old mistress, you know--the lady that father met last summer, who sent you and me five shillings each.”
“Oh! Mrs. Fowler. Of course, I know all about her. I wonder what she is writing to mother about.”
“Mother wrote to her last week,” said Harry; “you know she told father if ever he gave up the cab work she would like to know. I wonder what she says; run in and see, Dolly.”
Harry scrubbed away at Hotspur with a huish! huish! like any old hostler. In a few minutes Dolly came dancing into the stable.

“Oh! Harry, there never was anything so beautiful; Mrs. Fowler says we are all to go and live near her. There is a cottage now empty that will just suit us, with a garden and a henhouse, and apple-trees, and everything! and her coachman is going away in the spring, and then she will want father in his place; and there are good families round, where you can get a place in the garden or the stable, or as a page-boy; and there's a good school for me; and mother is laughing and crying by turns, and father does look so happy!”

“That's uncommon jolly,” said Harry, “and just the right thing, I should say; it will suit father and mother both; but I don't intend to be a page-boy with tight clothes and rows of buttons. I'll be a groom or a gardener.”
It was quickly settled that as soon as Jerry was well enough they should remove to the country, and that the cab and horses should be sold as soon as possible.

This was heavy news for me, for I was not young now, and could not look for any improvement in my condition. Since I left Birtwick I had never been so happy as with my dear master Jerry; but three years of cab work, even under the best conditions, will tell on one's strength, and I felt that I was not the horse that I had been.

Grant said at once that he would take Hotspur, and there were men on the stand who would have bought me; but Jerry said I should not go to cab work again with just anybody, and the governor promised to find a place for me where I should be comfortable.

The day came for going away. Jerry had not been allowed to go out yet, and I never saw him after that New Year's eve. Polly and the children came to bid me good-by. “Poor old Jack! dear old Jack! I wish we could take you with us,” she said, and then laying her hand on my mane she put her face close to my neck and kissed me. Dolly was crying and kissed me too. Harry stroked me a great deal, but said nothing, only he seemed very sad, and so I was led away to my new place.
translated_paragraphs: 对有些人来说，圣诞节和新年是十分欢乐的时节。可是对出租马车的车夫和拉车的马，那些日子虽有可能是个丰收季，却绝不是假日。聚会那么多，舞会那么多，开门营业的娱乐场所也那么多，活儿重，收得又常常很晚。有时车夫和马非得冒着雨，或顶着霜，在外面守上几个钟头，冻得直发抖，屋里的快活人却在乐声中跳个不停。我不知道那些漂亮的女士想没想过，车夫疲惫地坐在车座上等，他的马耐心地站着，直站到四条腿都冻僵了。
晚上的活这时大多落在我身上，因为我很惯于久站，杰里也更担心烈性子会受凉。圣诞节那一周，我们有许多活得干到深夜，杰里咳得很厉害。可不论几点回家，波莉总是守着不睡，提灯来迎接，满脸焦急和忧虑。
新年那天晚上，我们得送两位绅士到伦敦西区的一处广场去。九点钟，他们在一户人家门前下了车，吩咐我们十一点再来。“不过，”其中一个说，“是个牌局，你也许得多等那么几分钟。但千万别迟到。”
钟正敲十一下，我们就已到了门前。杰里向来守时。钟又敲过一刻，二刻，三刻，随后敲响十二下，大门一直没有打开。

白日里风向多变，一阵阵急雨扫过，此刻却变成了刺人的雨夹雪，好像从每一面吹来。冷得很，又没有地方遮挡。杰里从座位上下来，把我身上一条马毯重新往脖子上拉了拉。随后他来来回回走了几圈，一边走，一边跺脚。又想甩胳膊拍打取暖，才动两下，就引出一阵咳嗽。他便拉开车门，坐在车厢地板上，双脚搁在人行道上，这样稍能挡一挡风雪。钟仍旧每十五分钟响一次，门里始终没有人出来。十二点半，他去按了铃，问仆人今晚还要不要他候着。
“哦，那当然，准用得着你，”那人说，“你不能走，马上就该散了。”杰里又坐了下来，这时候他的嗓音已经嘶哑得我几乎听不见。
凌晨一点一刻，大门终于开了，两位绅士走出来，一句话不说就钻进车里，报了要去的地方，还有差不多两英里。我的四条腿已经冻麻，觉得几乎就要跌倒。那两人下车时，丝毫没有为叫我们等了这样久表示歉意，反而对车钱大为恼火。但杰里从不多收一文，也不肯少收一文，他们只好付了两个钟头又一刻钟的等候钱。这笔钱，杰里挣得可真苦。
我们终于回了家。他几乎开不了口，咳嗽的声音十分吓人。波莉什么也没问，只给他开好门，举着灯照亮。
“我能做点什么吗？”她问。
“好，先给杰克弄点暖和的吃，再替我熬一碗稀粥。”
这话是用沙哑的气声说出来的，他几乎喘不上气，可还是跟平常一样给我擦干了身子，甚至亲自爬上干草楼，又搬下一捆稻草给我铺床。波莉送来一份热乎乎的麸皮糊，我吃了很舒服。随后他们才锁上门走了。

次日上午已很迟了，才有人来到马厩，而且来的只有哈里。他替我俩梳洗、添料、打扫马栏，又把稻草铺回去，好像这天是星期日一样。他出奇地安静，没吹口哨，也没唱歌。中午他又来一趟，给我们吃的喝的，这次多莉跟着他。她在哭。我从他们彼此说的话听出来，杰里的病很危险，医生也说情况很重。这样过了两天，家中忧愁万分。我们只见到哈里，有时也见到多莉。我想她来是为了找个伴，因为波莉始终守在杰里身边，而他需要非常安静地休养。
第三天，哈里正在马厩里，外头有一阵轻轻的敲门声。格兰特头儿进来了。
“孩子，我没想到屋里去打扰，”他说，“只是想来问问你爸爸的病怎么样。”
“病得厉害，”哈里说，“差不多不能更糟了。他们管这叫‘支气管炎’。医生说，就看今夜，或是好转，或是朝另一头去。”
“不好，真不好，”格兰特摇摇头，“上星期我知道的就有两个人死于这个病。它取人命快得很。可只要人活着，就还有指望。你得提住这口气。”
“是啊，”哈里急急地说，“而且医生说，爸爸不喝酒，所以康复的希望比许多人大。他说昨天烧得那么高，爸爸要是平常喝酒，怕是会像一张纸那样给烧光了。可我想，医生心里觉得他能熬过来。您不也觉得他能吗，格兰特先生？”
头儿显得有些为难。
“孩子，这世上若有好人就该过得去这道难关的道理，那我确信他能过得去。他是我认识的最好的人。我明天一早还来看。”
第二天一清早，他果然来了。
“怎么样？”他问。
“爸爸好些了，”哈里说，“妈妈盼着他能熬过去。”
“感谢上帝！”头儿说，“现在你们要让他身上暖和，心里也不要有事忧虑。说到这儿，有两匹马得说一说。你瞧，杰克在暖和的厩里歇个一两星期，只有好处。你轻易就能领他上街来来回回走一趟，让他伸展四腿。可那个年轻的呢，要是没活做，没多久就会浑身上下都要往天上蹿，怎么说呢，你自己怕是招架不住。等他终于出了门，就要出意外。”
“现在已经这样了，”哈里说，“我已把他的谷料往少里喂，可他还是一身的劲，叫我不知拿他怎么办才好。”
“正是，”格兰特说，“你听我说，你告诉你母亲，她若不反对，我可以每天来领它出去，先这样办，等你们有了别的安排再说。我让它好好跑一趟活，赚来的钱，一半带来交给你母亲，足够贴补些马的饲料钱。你父亲参加的互助会很好，我知道，不过会里给的钱养不了马。这阵子它们单是嘴里消耗的，就要把自己吃穷了。中午我来听她怎么说。”不等哈里开口道谢，他已走了。
中午，我想他先去见了波莉，因为进马厩时他是同哈里一道来的。他们套上烈性子，把它带了出去。
往后一星期还多，他天天来领烈性子。哈里向他道谢或提起这份好心时，他只一笑置之，说这全是自己走运，他的马正好需要休息，换平时还得不到这点休息呢。
杰里的病稳稳好转，可医生说，他若想活到老，就再也不要回去赶出租马车。两个孩子常常凑在一处商量，不知道爸爸和妈妈该怎么办，又讨论他们自己能怎样帮着挣钱。
一天下午，烈性子被带回来，浑身又湿又脏。
“大街上尽是雪泥，”头儿说，“孩子，等你把他擦干弄干净，你自己也准会暖和起来。”
“放心吧，头儿，”哈里说，“在他干净、干爽以前，我可不走。您知道，我是爸爸教出来的。”
“要是所有男孩都能像你这样受过教就好了。”头儿说。
哈里正拿海绵擦去烈性子身上和腿上的泥，多莉走进来，脸上写着满满的心事。
“哈里，谁住在费尔斯托呀？妈妈收到一封从费尔斯托寄来的信，看来高兴得很，拿着就跑上楼找爸爸去了。”
“你不知道吗？那是福勒太太住处的名字呀。就是妈妈以前的女主人，记得吧？去年夏天爸爸遇见的那位太太，还给过咱俩一人五个先令。”
“哦，福勒太太！我当然知道她啦。我就想不通，她写信给妈妈是为的什么。”
“上星期妈妈先写过信给她，”哈里说，“你记不记得，她告诉过爸爸，要是有一天不再拉出租马车，要叫她知道。不知道她怎么回的话。快，多莉，跑进去瞧瞧吧。”
哈里继续给烈性子擦洗，嘴里“嗬咻，嗬咻”地招呼着，活像一个有年头的旅店马夫。过了几分钟，多莉蹦蹦跳跳回到马厩。
“哎呀，哈里，再没有比这更美的好事了！福勒太太说，让咱们全家搬到她附近住去。那儿眼下有座空小屋，正适合咱们，有花园，有鸡舍，有苹果树，什么都有！她的车夫春天要走，到时就需要爸爸去接他的班。周围有好些不错的人家，你可以找份花园或马厩里的差事，或者去做个小侍从。附近还有一所好学校，正好让我去！妈妈一会儿笑一会儿哭，爸爸看着简直高兴透了！”
“那真是好极了，”哈里说，“照我看，再合适不过，爸爸妈妈都会称心。可我不打算做什么小侍从，穿着紧窄的衣服，两排扣子一溜下去。我想做个马夫，或者做园丁。”
事情很快定下：只要杰里康复到能动身，他们就搬去乡间；出租马车和马则要尽快卖掉。
这对我是个沉重的消息。我已不再年轻，不会指望日子还能比现在好。离开伯特威克以后，我最幸福的时候，就是同亲爱的主人杰里在一起的这段时光。可是拉出租马车拉了三年，即便是在最好的条件下，也要耗费一匹马的力气。我感到自己已经不再是从前那匹马了。
格兰特当即说他肯买下烈性子。候客处也有人肯买我，可杰里说，不能把我随便交给什么人，又拉回去做出租马车的重活。头儿答应替我找一处可以舒服度日的地方。
动身的日子来到了，杰里仍没获准出门。自从那个新年之夜，我就没再见过他。波莉和孩子们来同我告别。“可怜的老杰克！亲爱的老杰克！我多盼能把你也一道带走啊。”她说着把手放在我的鬃毛上，脸贴着我的脖子，亲了我一下。多莉在哭，也吻了我。哈里抚摸了我好久，却一个字也没说，神色十分悲伤。随后，人们便牵我去了新的地方。

sections.title_zh: 第四部 / 第46章　杰克斯和一位女士
sections.title_en: Part IV / 46 Jakes and the Lady
source_paragraphs: I was sold to a corn dealer and baker, whom Jerry knew, and with him he thought I should have good food and fair work. In the first he was quite right, and if my master had always been on the premises I do not think I should have been overloaded, but there was a foreman who was always hurrying and driving every one, and frequently when I had quite a full load he would order something else to be taken on. My carter, whose name was Jakes, often said it was more than I ought to take, but the other always overruled him. “'Twas no use going twice when once would do, and he chose to get business forward.”

Jakes, like the other carters, always had the check-rein up, which prevented me from drawing easily, and by the time I had been there three or four months I found the work telling very much on my strength.

One day I was loaded more than usual, and part of the road was a steep uphill. I used all my strength, but I could not get on, and was obliged continually to stop. This did not please my driver, and he laid his whip on badly. “Get on, you lazy fellow,” he said, “or I'll make you.”

Again I started the heavy load, and struggled on a few yards; again the whip came down, and again I struggled forward. The pain of that great cart whip was sharp, but my mind was hurt quite as much as my poor sides. To be punished and abused when I was doing my very best was so hard it took the heart out of me. A third time he was flogging me cruelly, when a lady stepped quickly up to him, and said in a sweet, earnest voice:
“Oh! pray do not whip your good horse any more; I am sure he is doing all he can, and the road is very steep; I am sure he is doing his best.”
“If doing his best won't get this load up he must do something more than his best; that's all I know, ma'am,” said Jakes.
“But is it not a heavy load?” she said.

“Yes, yes, too heavy,” he said; “but that's not my fault; the foreman came just as we were starting, and would have three hundredweight more put on to save him trouble, and I must get on with it as well as I can.”
He was raising the whip again, when the lady said:
“Pray, stop; I think I can help you if you will let me.”
The man laughed.

“You see,” she said, “you do not give him a fair chance; he cannot use all his power with his head held back as it is with that check-rein; if you would take it off I am sure he would do better--do try it,” she said persuasively, “I should be very glad if you would.”
“Well, well,” said Jakes, with a short laugh, “anything to please a lady, of course. How far would you wish it down, ma'am?”
“Quite down, give him his head altogether.”
The rein was taken off, and in a moment I put my head down to my very knees. What a comfort it was! Then I tossed it up and down several times to get the aching stiffness out of my neck.
“Poor fellow! that is what you wanted,” said she, patting and stroking me with her gentle hand; “and now if you will speak kindly to him and lead him on I believe he will be able to do better.”

Jakes took the rein. “Come on, Blackie.” I put down my head, and threw my whole weight against the collar; I spared no strength; the load moved on, and I pulled it steadily up the hill, and then stopped to take breath.
The lady had walked along the footpath, and now came across into the road. She stroked and patted my neck, as I had not been patted for many a long day.

“You see he was quite willing when you gave him the chance; I am sure he is a fine-tempered creature, and I dare say has known better days. You won't put that rein on again, will you?” for he was just going to hitch it up on the old plan.

“Well, ma'am, I can't deny that having his head has helped him up the hill, and I'll remember it another time, and thank you, ma'am; but if he went without a check-rein I should be the laughing-stock of all the carters; it is the fashion, you see.”

“Is it not better,” she said, “to lead a good fashion than to follow a bad one? A great many gentlemen do not use check-reins now; our carriage horses have not worn them for fifteen years, and work with much less fatigue than those who have them; besides,” she added in a very serious voice, “we have no right to distress any of God's creatures without a very good reason; we call them dumb animals, and so they are, for they cannot tell us how they feel, but they do not suffer less because they have no words. But I must not detain you now; I thank you for trying my plan with your good horse, and I am sure you will find it far better than the whip. Good-day,” and with another soft pat on my neck she stepped lightly across the path, and I saw her no more.

“That was a real lady, I'll be bound for it,” said Jakes to himself; “she spoke just as polite as if I was a gentleman, and I'll try her plan, uphill, at any rate;” and I must do him the justice to say that he let my rein out several holes, and going uphill after that, he always gave me my head; but the heavy loads went on. Good feed and fair rest will keep up one's strength under full work, but no horse can stand against overloading; and I was getting so thoroughly pulled down from this cause that a younger horse was bought in my place. I may as well mention here what I suffered at this time from another cause. I had heard horses speak of it, but had never myself had experience of the evil; this was a badly-lighted stable; there was only one very small window at the end, and the consequence was that the stalls were almost dark.

Besides the depressing effect this had on my spirits, it very much weakened my sight, and when I was suddenly brought out of the darkness into the glare of daylight it was very painful to my eyes. Several times I stumbled over the threshold, and could scarcely see where I was going.

I believe, had I stayed there very long, I should have become purblind, and that would have been a great misfortune, for I have heard men say that a stone-blind horse was safer to drive than one which had imperfect sight, as it generally makes them very timid. However, I escaped without any permanent injury to my sight, and was sold to a large cab owner.
translated_paragraphs: 买下我的人是个粮商，兼做面包生意。杰里认得他，想我到了他那儿会有好吃食，担子也会公道。前一点他看得很准。如果我的新主人始终会待在店铺里，我想他们也不至于叫我拉得太重，可有个领班成天催促这个、驱赶那个，往往看我已经装得满满的，还要额外加上别的。我那赶车的人叫杰克斯，时常说分量已超过我该拉的了，却每回都让领班顶回去。“一趟能办完的事，干吗要走两趟？他就是要让生意往前赶。”
杰克斯和别的赶货车的人一样，总把吊缰往上扣，使我不能宽松自在地拉车。到了他那里三四个月以后，我已感到这活计大大损耗着我的力气。
一天，我身后的货比平常还重，偏又有一段陡峭的上坡。我用尽全部力气，也不能一直往上拉，不得不时常停下。车夫很不高兴，狠狠给我吃了几鞭子。“往前走，你这个懒东西！”他说，“要不看我怎么逼你走！”
我又一次拖动沉重的货车，勉强向前挣出几码。鞭子又一次落在身上，我又一次拼命往前。那条货车夫的粗鞭子抽在身上，疼得很尖锐，可我心里的伤痛一点也不比可怜的两胁轻。明明已经尽了最大的力气，还要这样挨打受骂，实在太不公平，都快叫我丧失信心了。他第三次狠命抽打我时，一位女士快步走向前，用温柔而认真的声音说：
“哎呀，求你别再抽你的好马了！我敢说它已经使尽气力，这坡又那么陡。我敢说，它已把能做的都做到了。”
“尽了力还拉不上去，它就得比尽力再多做一点。我只知道这个，太太。”杰克斯说。
“不过，这一车难道不重吗？”她说。
“重，重，太重了，”他说，“不过这又不是我的错。我们正要出发，领班来了，为了他自己省事，硬要再往上装三英担。我也只能竭力把它弄走了。”
他正又把鞭子举起来，那位女士说：
“请先住手。只要你愿意，我想我能帮你。”
车夫笑了一声。
“你瞧，”她说，“你没让它有个好好出力的机会。头给那道吊缰往后扯住，使不上全部力气。你若肯把它解开，我敢说它会拉得好些。请试一试吧，”她劝道，“你要肯试，我会很高兴。”
“好吧，好吧，”杰克斯短促地笑了一声，“当然，为叫女士称心，什么都能做。太太，您想让我把缰绳放低多少？”
“完全放下来，把头整个放开，交还给它自己。”
缰绳解开了。转眼之间，我的头已经低到了自己的膝头。那是怎样的舒畅！我把脖子上下挥动了好几回，好松走积在颈间那又痛又僵的感觉。
“可怜的家伙！你要的就是这个呀。”她柔软的手在我脖子上一阵轻拍、抚摸，“现在只要肯好好招呼它，领它往前，我相信它一定做得更好。”
杰克斯拿起缰绳。“来，小黑。”我低下头，将全身重量抵向挽车的颈圈，所有力气一分也没留。重车动了，我稳稳地把它拉上坡顶，这才停下来喘气。
那位女士一直沿人行道跟着走，现在从小道横到大路上。她摸摸、拍拍我的脖子。好久好久，都没有人那样拍过我了。
“你看，你一让它有机会，它是肯出力的。我敢说它脾气极好，以前大约过过更好的日子。你不会再把那道缰扣上了吧？”因为杰克斯正准备照老办法把它挂回去。
“嗯，太太，我不能否认，刚才让它自由低头，在上坡时确实有用，这件事我往后会记得。谢谢您，太太。不过它要是一道吊缰也不戴，我就成了所有车夫的笑柄。您瞧，那是时髦。”

“自己带头兴一种好风气，”她说，“难道不比跟着别人赶一种坏时髦好吗？如今许多绅士已经不用吊缰了。我们家的车马有十五年不戴，干起活来，比戴着吊缰的马少费许多力。何况，”她又很认真地加上一句，“若没有十分充分的理由，我们无权叫上帝所造的生灵受苦。我们称它们是不能说话的兽，它们也确实没有话语可以告诉我们心里的感受。可不能说，不等于它们少受一分苦。我不能再耽搁你的时间了。谢谢你肯在这匹好马上试一试我的办法。我相信你会发现，它比鞭子好用得多。再见。”她又柔柔地拍了我一下，轻轻巧巧横过小路去了，从此我再没有看见她。

“我敢打赌，这才是一位真正的女士，”杰克斯自言自语，“她跟我说话客客气气，倒像我也是位绅士。我要试试她的办法，至少爬坡时试。”我得替他说句公道话，他的确给我的吊缰放松了好几个扣眼。自此以后，凡是上坡，他也总给我松开，让我能低头。只是重担仍旧那么重。只要有好饲料，有适当的休息，一匹马做够分量的活，还是能保住力气。可超出负荷，没有哪一匹马能受得住。为这个缘故，我虚弱到几乎撑不下去，他们便买了一匹年轻的马来接替我。在这里，不妨顺带说说那期间另一样东西给我带来的苦处。以前我听别的马谈过，自己从未亲身领教，那就是不见光的马厩。整座厩只有尽头一扇极小的窗，结果是马栏里差不多一片黑暗。
这不但叫我精神抑郁，也大大削弱了我的眼力。一下子被人从黑暗中牵到耀眼的日光下，两眼会十分疼痛。有几次我在门槛上绊了一下，几乎看不清自己走的方向。
我相信，若在那里再住很久，我会变成半瞎。那可是很大的不幸。我听人说过，完全失明的马，反而比看东西模糊的马驾起来更稳妥，因为视物不清，往往会叫马格外胆怯。我到底逃过了，眼睛没留下永久的伤害，随后被卖给一个有大批出租马车的老板。

sections.title_zh: 第四部 / 第47章　艰难时世
source_paragraphs: My new master I shall never forget; he had black eyes and a hooked nose, his mouth was as full of teeth as a bull-dog's, and his voice was as harsh as the grinding of cart wheels over graveled stones. His name was Nicholas Skinner, and I believe he was the man that poor Seedy Sam drove for.
I have heard men say that seeing is believing; but I should say that feeling is believing; for much as I had seen before, I never knew till now the utter misery of a cab-horse's life.
Skinner had a low set of cabs and a low set of drivers; he was hard on the men, and the men were hard on the horses. In this place we had no Sunday rest, and it was in the heat of summer.

Sometimes on a Sunday morning a party of fast men would hire the cab for the day; four of them inside and another with the driver, and I had to take them ten or fifteen miles out into the country, and back again; never would any of them get down to walk up a hill, let it be ever so steep, or the day ever so hot--unless, indeed, when the driver was afraid I should not manage it, and sometimes I was so fevered and worn that I could hardly touch my food. How I used to long for the nice bran mash with niter in it that Jerry used to give us on Saturday nights in hot weather, that used to cool us down and make us so comfortable. Then we had two nights and a whole day for unbroken rest, and on Monday morning we were as fresh as young horses again; but here there was no rest, and my driver was just as hard as his master. He had a cruel whip with something so sharp at the end that it sometimes drew blood, and he would even whip me under the belly, and flip the lash out at my head. Indignities like these took the heart out of me terribly, but still I did my best and never hung back; for, as poor Ginger said, it was no use; men are the strongest.
My life was now so utterly wretched that I wished I might, like Ginger, drop down dead at my work and be out of my misery, and one day my wish very nearly came to pass.

I went on the stand at eight in the morning, and had done a good share of work, when we had to take a fare to the railway. A long train was just expected in, so my driver pulled up at the back of some of the outside cabs to take the chance of a return fare. It was a very heavy train, and as all the cabs were soon engaged ours was called for. There was a party of four; a noisy, blustering man with a lady, a little boy and a young girl, and a great deal of luggage. The lady and the boy got into the cab, and while the man ordered about the luggage the young girl came and looked at me.
“Papa,” she said, “I am sure this poor horse cannot take us and all our luggage so far, he is so very weak and worn up. Do look at him.”
“Oh! he's all right, miss,” said my driver, “he's strong enough.”
The porter, who was pulling about some heavy boxes, suggested to the gentleman, as there was so much luggage, whether he would not take a second cab.
“Can your horse do it, or can't he?” said the blustering man.
“Oh! he can do it all right, sir; send up the boxes, porter; he could take more than that;” and he helped to haul up a box so heavy that I could feel the springs go down.
“Papa, papa, do take a second cab,” said the young girl in a beseeching tone. “I am sure we are wrong, I am sure it is very cruel.”

“Nonsense, Grace, get in at once, and don't make all this fuss; a pretty thing it would be if a man of business had to examine every cab-horse before he hired it--the man knows his own business of course; there, get in and hold your tongue!”

My gentle friend had to obey, and box after box was dragged up and lodged on the top of the cab or settled by the side of the driver. At last all was ready, and with his usual jerk at the rein and slash of the whip he drove out of the station.
The load was very heavy and I had had neither food nor rest since morning; but I did my best, as I always had done, in spite of cruelty and injustice.

I got along fairly till we came to Ludgate Hill; but there the heavy load and my own exhaustion were too much. I was struggling to keep on, goaded by constant chucks of the rein and use of the whip, when in a single moment--I cannot tell how--my feet slipped from under me, and I fell heavily to the ground on my side; the suddenness and the force with which I fell seemed to beat all the breath out of my body. I lay perfectly still; indeed, I had no power to move, and I thought now I was going to die. I heard a sort of confusion round me, loud, angry voices, and the getting down of the luggage, but it was all like a dream. I thought I heard that sweet, pitiful voice saying, “Oh! that poor horse! it is all our fault.” Some one came and loosened the throat strap of my bridle, and undid the traces which kept the collar so tight upon me. Some one said, “He's dead, he'll never get up again.” Then I could hear a policeman giving orders, but I did not even open my eyes; I could only draw a gasping breath now and then. Some cold water was thrown over my head, and some cordial was poured into my mouth, and something was covered over me. I cannot tell how long I lay there, but I found my life coming back, and a kind-voiced man was patting me and encouraging me to rise. After some more cordial had been given me, and after one or two attempts, I staggered to my feet, and was gently led to some stables which were close by. Here I was put into a well-littered stall, and some warm gruel was brought to me, which I drank thankfully.

In the evening I was sufficiently recovered to be led back to Skinner's stables, where I think they did the best for me they could. In the morning Skinner came with a farrier to look at me. He examined me very closely and said:
“This is a case of overwork more than disease, and if you could give him a run off for six months he would be able to work again; but now there is not an ounce of strength left in him.”

“Then he must just go to the dogs,” said Skinner. “I have no meadows to nurse sick horses in--he might get well or he might not; that sort of thing don't suit my business; my plan is to work 'em as long as they'll go, and then sell 'em for what they'll fetch, at the knacker's or elsewhere.”

“If he was broken-winded,” said the farrier, “you had better have him killed out of hand, but he is not; there is a sale of horses coming off in about ten days; if you rest him and feed him up he may pick up, and you may get more than his skin is worth, at any rate.”

Upon this advice Skinner, rather unwillingly, I think, gave orders that I should be well fed and cared for, and the stable man, happily for me, carried out the orders with a much better will than his master had in giving them. Ten days of perfect rest, plenty of good oats, hay, bran mashes, with boiled linseed mixed in them, did more to get up my condition than anything else could have done; those linseed mashes were delicious, and I began to think, after all, it might be better to live than go to the dogs. When the twelfth day after the accident came, I was taken to the sale, a few miles out of London. I felt that any change from my present place must be an improvement, so I held up my head, and hoped for the best.
translated_paragraphs: 我的新主人，我永远忘不了。他生着黑眼睛、鹰钩鼻，一张嘴张开，满口的牙齿好像斗牛犬。说话的声音刺耳粗涩，像大车轮子碾着砂砾磨过去。他名叫尼古拉斯·斯金纳，我相信，可怜的落魄萨姆就是替他拉车的。
我听人说，眼见为实。可依我看，亲身领受才会真懂。虽然从前我已经目睹了许多，但一匹出租马车的马可以活得何等凄苦，直到现在我才真正知道。
斯金纳手里的马车低劣，手下的一群车夫也粗鄙。他对车夫苛刻，车夫便对马苛刻。在这里，星期日没有休息。时节又是酷暑。

有些星期日的早晨，一群寻欢作乐的男人租下车一整天。四个坐在里面，另一个跟车夫坐在一起。我得带着他们到十英里或十五英里以外的乡下去，再拉着回来。不论坡有多陡，天气多热，没有一个人肯下车走一段，除非车夫自己也怕我拉不上去。有时我浑身发热，疲惫得几乎碰不了饲料。天热时，每逢周六晚上杰里会给我们的那一顿麸皮糊，拌着一点硝石，多么叫人想念啊！吃了它，我们就凉爽、舒坦起来。随后还有两个夜晚和一个完整的白天，不被打扰地休息。到了周一早上，我们又像年轻的马那样精神振奋。可眼下没有休息，驾我的人也跟他的主人一样心硬。他有条残忍的鞭，梢上不知装着什么尖利的东西，有时一鞭便能见血。他甚至会抽我肚子底下，也会将鞭梢朝我的头面甩来。这类侮辱使我分外灰心。尽管如此，我依然尽力，不曾故意不肯向前。正如可怜的姜儿说过的，那没有用。人比我们有力量。
如今我的日子实在悲惨，我真盼着能像姜儿那样，在拉车的时候一头倒下死去，好就此脱离苦海。有一天，我这个愿望差一点就成真了。
我早晨八点到站上候客，已经干了不小的一份活，又接到一单，要把乘客送去火车站。正有一趟很长的列车快要进站，车夫便在站外那一排出租马车后面停了下来，想碰碰回程接客的运气。这趟车载客极多，所有出租马车很快都有了生意，也有人来叫我们的车。这是一行四人，一个嗓门很响、动辄吹胡子瞪眼的男人，带着一位太太、一个小男孩、一个少女，还有大堆的行李。太太和男孩坐上车，男人指挥人安置行李，那个姑娘却走过来看我。
“爸爸，”她说，“这匹马又虚弱，又累成这样。我敢说它没法带着我们，还有这么多行李，走那么远的路。您看看它呀。”
“哦，它没事，小姐，”我的车夫说，“力气很够。”
脚夫正搬着几只沉箱子。他见行李实在太多，便向那先生提议，要不要另叫第二辆车。
“你的马究竟拉得动，还是拉不动？”那个气势汹汹的男人问。
“哦，拉得动，先生，准没问题。脚夫，箱子递上来，更多些它也拉得动。”他又帮忙拽上一只箱子，沉得我都感觉到车子的弹簧被压了下去。
“爸爸，爸爸，求您再叫一辆车吧，”少女用恳求的口气说，“我们这样做一定不对，一定很残忍。”
“胡闹，格蕾丝！马上上车，别这么大惊小怪。生意人若每回叫一辆出租马车之前，还得先把马检查一遍，那可真是桩奇闻。车夫当然懂他自己的行当。好了，进去，别再开口！”
我那温柔的朋友只得听从。箱子一只接一只被拖上去，或搁在车顶，或安置到车夫身边。终于一切就绪，他照例使劲一抖缰，猛地一挥鞭，赶我出了车站。
载荷很重，我又从早到现在，既没吃过东西，也没歇过脚。但一向如此，不管别人怎样粗暴，怎样待我不公，我仍然尽了自己的力。

直到拉德盖特山坡前，我还走得勉强过得去。可到了那里，身后的重压，加上我本身已然力竭，再也撑不住了。车夫不停扯缰、抽鞭催我，我挣扎着想再往前去。忽然之间——我也说不上究竟是怎样——四蹄从身下打滑，我侧着身子重重摔倒在路面。那一下来得那么突然、那么猛烈，仿佛连身体里仅有的气也一并摔出去了。我一动不动地躺着。我的确没有力气动，心想这回是要死了。隐约听见四周一片混乱，有人气愤地大声说话，有人在把行李搬下车来，一切好像隔着一场梦。似乎又听见那个温和、怜惜我的声音在说：“啊，那匹可怜的马！全是我们的过错。”有人走来，松开我笼头喉下的皮带，又解下挽索，把勒得那么紧的颈圈放松。有人说：“死了。它起不来了。”又听见警察在下命令。我连眼皮都没睁开，只能隔一阵艰难地吸一口气。有人往我头上泼了些冷水，将某种提神的药液倒进我嘴里，又有东西遮盖在我身上。我不知道自己这样躺了多久，不过感觉到生命正在一点点回来。有个声音亲切的人拍着我，鼓励我站起。他们又喂了一些药液。我试了一两次，总算摇摇晃晃站稳，让人轻轻牵到很近的一座马厩。那里有个垫草铺得厚实的马栏等着我，还有一份温热的稀粥。我怀着感激，把它喝了下去。
到傍晚，我恢复了些力气，足够让人领回斯金纳的马厩。我想，在那里他们也尽可能照料了我。早晨，斯金纳带来一位马医。马医把我从头到脚检查得十分仔细，开口说：
“它的情形与其说是害病，不如说是干活干过了头。如果能把它放出去休养六个月，还能再干活。可眼下，它身上连最后一点力气都没了。”
“那就只能让它去喂狗了，”斯金纳说，“我没有草场专给病马养身子。它也许好得了，也许好不了。那种事跟我的生意合不来。我的做法是，只要还能走，就继续使。末了，能卖多少卖多少，卖去宰马场也好，卖去别的地方也好。”
“若是它的肺气已经坏了，”马医说，“最好索性现在就让它死。可它没有。大约十天后有场卖马的集市。你先叫它休息，给足饲料，或许能缓过来。总之卖的时候，总有希望比一张马皮值钱些。”

听了这个主意，斯金纳便吩咐人好好喂养、照看我。我觉得他很不情愿；然而幸而替我操持的马夫，遵照吩咐做起来，比发出吩咐的主人热心得多。十天完全歇息，有充足的好燕麦、干草，还有拌了煮熟的亚麻籽的麸皮糊。叫我的气力和样貌好转起来，没有什么能比得过这些。亚麻籽糊格外香，我又开始想，说到底，活着也许总比被拖去喂狗要好。出事以后第十二天，他们牵着我去赴马市，地点在伦敦城外几英里。我心想，不管换去哪里，都一定比现在的地方好。于是我昂着头，盼望能有个好结果。

sections.title_zh: 第四部 / 第48章　农场主瑟拉古德和孙子威利
sections.title_en: Part IV / 48 Farmer Thoroughgood and His Grandson Willie
source_paragraphs: At this sale, of course I found myself in company with the old broken-down horses--some lame, some broken-winded, some old, and some that I am sure it would have been merciful to shoot.

The buyers and sellers, too, many of them, looked not much better off than the poor beasts they were bargaining about. There were poor old men, trying to get a horse or a pony for a few pounds, that might drag about some little wood or coal cart. There were poor men trying to sell a worn-out beast for two or three pounds, rather than have the greater loss of killing him. Some of them looked as if poverty and hard times had hardened them all over; but there were others that I would have willingly used the last of my strength in serving; poor and shabby, but kind and human, with voices that I could trust. There was one tottering old man who took a great fancy to me, and I to him, but I was not strong enough--it was an anxious time! Coming from the better part of the fair, I noticed a man who looked like a gentleman farmer, with a young boy by his side; he had a broad back and round shoulders, a kind, ruddy face, and he wore a broad-brimmed hat. When he came up to me and my companions he stood still and gave a pitiful look round upon us. I saw his eye rest on me; I had still a good mane and tail, which did something for my appearance. I pricked my ears and looked at him.
“There's a horse, Willie, that has known better days.”
“Poor old fellow!” said the boy, “do you think, grandpapa, he was ever a carriage horse?”

“Oh, yes! my boy,” said the farmer, coming closer, “he might have been anything when he was young; look at his nostrils and his ears, the shape of his neck and shoulder; there's a deal of breeding about that horse.” He put out his hand and gave me a kind pat on the neck. I put out my nose in answer to his kindness; the boy stroked my face.
“Poor old fellow! see, grandpapa, how well he understands kindness. Could not you buy him and make him young again as you did with Ladybird?”
“My dear boy, I can't make all old horses young; besides, Ladybird was not so very old, as she was run down and badly used.”

“Well, grandpapa, I don't believe that this one is old; look at his mane and tail. I wish you would look into his mouth, and then you could tell; though he is so very thin, his eyes are not sunk like some old horses'.”
The old gentleman laughed. “Bless the boy! he is as horsey as his old grandfather.”
“But do look at his mouth, grandpapa, and ask the price; I am sure he would grow young in our meadows.”
The man who had brought me for sale now put in his word.

“The young gentleman's a real knowing one, sir. Now the fact is, this 'ere hoss is just pulled down with overwork in the cabs; he's not an old one, and I heerd as how the vetenary should say, that a six months' run off would set him right up, being as how his wind was not broken. I've had the tending of him these ten days past, and a gratefuller, pleasanter animal I never met with, and 'twould be worth a gentleman's while to give a five-pound note for him, and let him have a chance. I'll be bound he'd be worth twenty pounds next spring.”
The old gentleman laughed, and the little boy looked up eagerly.
“Oh, grandpapa, did you not say the colt sold for five pounds more than you expected? You would not be poorer if you did buy this one.”
The farmer slowly felt my legs, which were much swelled and strained; then he looked at my mouth. “Thirteen or fourteen, I should say; just trot him out, will you?”
I arched my poor thin neck, raised my tail a little, and threw out my legs as well as I could, for they were very stiff.
“What is the lowest you will take for him?” said the farmer as I came back.
“Five pounds, sir; that was the lowest price my master set.”

“'Tis a speculation,” said the old gentleman, shaking his head, but at the same time slowly drawing out his purse, “quite a speculation! Have you any more business here?” he said, counting the sovereigns into his hand.
“No, sir, I can take him for you to the inn, if you please.”
“Do so, I am now going there.”

They walked forward, and I was led behind. The boy could hardly control his delight, and the old gentleman seemed to enjoy his pleasure. I had a good feed at the inn, and was then gently ridden home by a servant of my new master's, and turned into a large meadow with a shed in one corner of it.

Mr. Thoroughgood, for that was the name of my benefactor, gave orders that I should have hay and oats every night and morning, and the run of the meadow during the day, and, “you, Willie,” said he, “must take the oversight of him; I give him in charge to you.”

The boy was proud of his charge, and undertook it in all seriousness. There was not a day when he did not pay me a visit; sometimes picking me out from among the other horses, and giving me a bit of carrot, or something good, or sometimes standing by me while I ate my oats. He always came with kind words and caresses, and of course I grew very fond of him. He called me Old Crony, as I used to come to him in the field and follow him about. Sometimes he brought his grandfather, who always looked closely at my legs.
“This is our point, Willie,” he would say; “but he is improving so steadily that I think we shall see a change for the better in the spring.”

The perfect rest, the good food, the soft turf, and gentle exercise, soon began to tell on my condition and my spirits. I had a good constitution from my mother, and I was never strained when I was young, so that I had a better chance than many horses who have been worked before they came to their full strength. During the winter my legs improved so much that I began to feel quite young again. The spring came round, and one day in March Mr. Thoroughgood determined that he would try me in the phaeton. I was well pleased, and he and Willie drove me a few miles. My legs were not stiff now, and I did the work with perfect ease.
“He's growing young, Willie; we must give him a little gentle work now, and by mid-summer he will be as good as Ladybird. He has a beautiful mouth and good paces; they can't be better.”
“Oh, grandpapa, how glad I am you bought him!”
“So am I, my boy; but he has to thank you more than me; we must now be looking out for a quiet, genteel place for him, where he will be valued.”
translated_paragraphs: 到了这场马市，自然，我被归到衰老残弱的马那边。有的瘸了，有的肺气坏了，有的是年纪大了。还有些，我敢肯定，给它们一枪叫它们不再受苦，才是仁慈。

那些买家和卖家，看上去也有许多并不比他们讨价还价的可怜牲口好到哪儿去。有些穷老头想用几英镑买一匹马或小矮马，好拉着一辆载柴或载煤的小车四处兜售。有些穷人来卖耗尽了的牲口，宁可换得两三英镑，不愿把它宰掉、亏得更多。有些人看着像是让贫穷和艰难的日子磨得浑身上下都变硬了。可也有些人，我情愿把剩下的最后一点气力用来替他们服务。他们虽贫穷寒酸，却和善、有人情味，声音是我信得过的。有一位走路颤颤巍巍的老人很喜欢我，我也喜欢他。只可惜我力气还不够。那真是叫我焦虑的时光！有个人从马市上较好的一头走过来，我留意到他像是位家境不错的农场主，身边有个小男孩。他脊背宽厚，肩膀浑圆，一张红润和气的脸，头戴宽檐帽。他走到我和其他马的跟前，站住，满怀怜悯地四下望望。我看见他的目光停在我身上。我还剩着一副好鬃毛、好尾巴，多少替我撑着点样貌。我竖起耳朵，也望着他。
“威利，看这一匹，它准是过过好日子的。”
“可怜的老伙计！”男孩说，“爷爷，您想它以前有没有拉过体面人家的马车？”
“哦，有的，孩子，”农场主走近些说，“他年轻的时候，想做什么大概都做得好。看看他的鼻孔，看看那双耳朵，还有颈子和肩的形状。这匹马的血统可不一般。”他伸出手来，在我脖子上亲切地拍了拍。我也把鼻子凑过去，答谢他的好意。男孩抚摸着我的脸。
“可怜的老伙计！爷爷，您瞧，他多明白谁待他好。您能不能把他买下来，像上回照管小瓢虫那样，叫他重新年轻起来呢？”
“好孩子，我哪能把所有老马都变年轻？何况小瓢虫也不是那么老，只不过让人使唤过了头，又受过虐待。”
“可是，爷爷，我也不相信这一匹就老啊。您瞧它的鬃毛，瞧它的尾巴。要是您肯瞧瞧它的嘴，就知道究竟多大了。它虽然很瘦，两只眼睛却不像有些老马那样陷进去。”
老先生笑了。“这孩子哟！喜欢起马来，跟他这老爷爷一个样。”
“不过您就看看它的嘴吧，爷爷，再问问价钱。我敢肯定，它到了咱们的草场，能慢慢变年轻的。”
带我来卖的人这时也插进一句话。
“这位小少爷真懂行，先生。事情明摆着，这马是叫拉出租马车的活给累垮的。年纪可还不算老。听人家说，马医的原话，它要能在草地上歇半年，保管就能挺起来，因为它的肺气没有坏。这十来天都是我照管它。这样和气、这样知道感激的马，我还没遇着过。要是有哪位老爷肯赏五英镑，给它一个机会，绝对值得。等到明年春天，我敢打保票，它准值二十英镑。”
老先生笑了，小男孩急切地仰脸望着他。
“哎呀，爷爷，您不是说，上回那匹小马驹卖出的价钱，比您原想的多了五英镑？就算您把这一匹买下来，钱也不比原来少呀。”
农场主不紧不慢摸了摸我的腿。那时我的腿肿得厉害，筋骨也有拉伤。随后他看了看我的嘴。“我估摸十三岁到十四岁，”他说，“领它出去小跑一圈，行不行？”
我弓起瘦瘦的脖子，尾巴也稍稍翘了起来。我的腿僵得很，可我还是尽力伸开步子给他看。
我跑回来时，农场主问：“你这匹马，最低多少肯卖？”
“五英镑，先生。我家主人定的最低就是这个价。”
“这是押一笔不知输赢的钱啊，”老先生说着摇了摇头，与此同时却已慢慢掏出了钱袋，“真叫人不知道输赢。你在市上还有别的要办吗？”他一面问，一面把几枚一镑的金币数进对方手里。
“没有，先生。要是您愿意，我可以替您把它牵到客栈。”
“那就这么办，我现在也往那里去。”
爷孙俩走在前面，我让人牵着跟在后头。男孩几乎藏不住自己的欣喜，老先生看他开心，自己也显得很受用。我在客栈吃了丰盛的一顿，又由新主人的一个仆人温和地骑着回去。随后他们把我放进一大片草场，角上有一座棚子。
帮助我的这位恩人名叫瑟拉古德先生。他吩咐，每天早晚都要给我喂干草和燕麦，白天要让我在草场上自由活动。“至于你，威利，”他说，“就由你把这些事盯好。我把他交给你照管。”
男孩十分以自己的差事为荣，办起事来也一丝不苟。没有哪一天他不来探望我。有时他从其他马当中把我找出来，给一片胡萝卜，或是别的好吃的。有时我吃燕麦，他就站在我身旁。每趟总带来几声好话和一番爱抚，我自然日益喜欢他。我常在草场上主动走近他，他走到哪里，我跟到哪里，他便叫我“老伙伴”。偶尔他还会领祖父一起来，老人总仔仔细细打量我的腿。
“咱们最得留心的是这里，威利，”他常说，“不过他在一点点稳步好转，照这样到明春，我想就会看出真正的起色。”

充分的休息、丰足的好饲料、柔软的草皮、温和的活动，很快就在我的身体和精神上见了成效。我从母亲那里得来一副好体格，年轻时又从没人过早勉强我出力。所以，比起那些力气没长足便被使唤的马，我有更好的机会康复。整个冬天，我的腿进步了许多，都开始觉得自己当真重新年轻了。春天又来。三月的一天，瑟拉古德先生决定给我套上敞式四轮轻车试试。我很乐意。爷爷跟威利驾着我走了几英里。现在我的四腿一点也不僵，干这份活，轻松得很。
“他正越活越年轻呢，威利。现在咱们得给他一点轻快活儿干。等到仲夏，他会跟小瓢虫一样好。他的嘴真灵，步子也好，再也挑不出更好的。”
“啊，爷爷，您买下他，我太高兴了！”
“我也高兴，我的孩子。不过，这匹马更该谢的人是你。现在咱们得留心，给他找个清静体面的人家，能真心拿他当回事。”

sections.title_zh: 第四部 / 第49章　我最后的家
source_paragraphs: One day during this summer the groom cleaned and dressed me with such extraordinary care that I thought some new change must be at hand; he trimmed my fetlocks and legs, passed the tarbrush over my hoofs, and even parted my forelock. I think the harness had an extra polish. Willie seemed half-anxious, half-merry, as he got into the chaise with his grandfather.
“If the ladies take to him,” said the old gentleman, “they'll be suited and he'll be suited. We can but try.”

At the distance of a mile or two from the village we came to a pretty, low house, with a lawn and shrubbery at the front and a drive up to the door. Willie rang the bell, and asked if Miss Blomefield or Miss Ellen was at home. Yes, they were. So, while Willie stayed with me, Mr. Thoroughgood went into the house. In about ten minutes he returned, followed by three ladies; one tall, pale lady, wrapped in a white shawl, leaned on a younger lady, with dark eyes and a merry face; the other, a very stately-looking person, was Miss Blomefield. They all came and looked at me and asked questions. The younger lady--that was Miss Ellen--took to me very much; she said she was sure she should like me, I had such a good face. The tall, pale lady said that she should always be nervous in riding behind a horse that had once been down, as I might come down again, and if I did she should never get over the fright.

“You see, ladies,” said Mr. Thoroughgood, “many first-rate horses have had their knees broken through the carelessness of their drivers without any fault of their own, and from what I see of this horse I should say that is his case; but of course I do not wish to influence you. If you incline you can have him on trial, and then your coachman will see what he thinks of him.”

“You have always been such a good adviser to us about our horses,” said the stately lady, “that your recommendation would go a long way with me, and if my sister Lavinia sees no objection we will accept your offer of a trial, with thanks.”
It was then arranged that I should be sent for the next day.
In the morning a smart-looking young man came for me. At first he looked pleased; but when he saw my knees he said in a disappointed voice:
“I didn't think, sir, you would have recommended my ladies a blemished horse like that.”

“'Handsome is that handsome does',” said my master; “you are only taking him on trial, and I am sure you will do fairly by him, young man. If he is not as safe as any horse you ever drove send him back.”
I was led to my new home, placed in a comfortable stable, fed, and left to myself. The next day, when the groom was cleaning my face, he said:
“That is just like the star that 'Black Beauty' had; he is much the same height, too. I wonder where he is now.”
A little further on he came to the place in my neck where I was bled and where a little knot was left in the skin. He almost started, and began to look me over carefully, talking to himself.

“White star in the forehead, one white foot on the off side, this little knot just in that place;” then looking at the middle of my back--“and, as I am alive, there is that little patch of white hair that John used to call 'Beauty's three-penny bit'. It must be 'Black Beauty'! Why, Beauty! Beauty! do you know me?--little Joe Green, that almost killed you?” And he began patting and patting me as if he was quite overjoyed.

I could not say that I remembered him, for now he was a fine grown young fellow, with black whiskers and a man's voice, but I was sure he knew me, and that he was Joe Green, and I was very glad. I put my nose up to him, and tried to say that we were friends. I never saw a man so pleased.

“Give you a fair trial! I should think so indeed! I wonder who the rascal was that broke your knees, my old Beauty! you must have been badly served out somewhere; well, well, it won't be my fault if you haven't good times of it now. I wish John Manly was here to see you.”

In the afternoon I was put into a low park chair and brought to the door. Miss Ellen was going to try me, and Green went with her. I soon found that she was a good driver, and she seemed pleased with my paces. I heard Joe telling her about me, and that he was sure I was Squire Gordon's old “Black Beauty”.
When we returned the other sisters came out to hear how I had behaved myself. She told them what she had just heard, and said:
“I shall certainly write to Mrs. Gordon, and tell her that her favorite horse has come to us. How pleased she will be!”

After this I was driven every day for a week or so, and as I appeared to be quite safe, Miss Lavinia at last ventured out in the small close carriage. After this it was quite decided to keep me and call me by my old name of “Black Beauty”.

I have now lived in this happy place a whole year. Joe is the best and kindest of grooms. My work is easy and pleasant, and I feel my strength and spirits all coming back again. Mr. Thoroughgood said to Joe the other day:
“In your place he will last till he is twenty years old--perhaps more.”

Willie always speaks to me when he can, and treats me as his special friend. My ladies have promised that I shall never be sold, and so I have nothing to fear; and here my story ends. My troubles are all over, and I am at home; and often before I am quite awake, I fancy I am still in the orchard at Birtwick, standing with my old friends under the apple-trees.
translated_paragraphs: 那年夏天，有一天，马夫格外仔细地给我梳洗。我心想，怕是又要有什么变动。他修了我的腿毛和球节毛，给蹄子涂上松焦油，连额前的鬃毛都分了一条缝。我看挽具也比平时多擦过一遍。威利和他爷爷坐进马车时，神情一半是高兴，一半有些担心。
“要是几位小姐喜欢它，她们就有合适的马，它也有合适的家。总可以试试。”老先生说。
离村子一两英里，有座漂亮的矮房子，门前是草坪、灌木和直达门口的车道。威利按了铃，问布洛姆菲尔德小姐或是埃伦小姐在不在家。她们都在。他留下陪我，瑟拉古德先生先进了屋。大约十分钟，他带了三位女士走出来。一位高高瘦瘦的，脸色苍白，披着白披肩，搭着一位年轻姑娘的胳膊。年轻姑娘黑眼睛，一张快活的脸。另一位仪态庄重，便是布洛姆菲尔德小姐。
三位都走上来看我，问了好些话。年轻的埃伦小姐一眼就喜欢上我，说我面相好，她准会喜欢我。苍白的那位说，坐一匹跌倒过的马拉的车，她总要不安，怕我再跌一跤。我要是真跌了，她恐怕再也缓不过那口气。
“女士们，许多一等一的好马，都因为车夫不小心，跌坏了膝盖，马自己一点儿过错也没有。照我看，这匹马正是这种情形。”瑟拉古德先生说，“当然我无意左右你们。你们愿意的话，让它来试做几天，车夫自然看得出好不好。”
庄重的小姐说：“向您讨教马的事，我们一向受益。您愿意推荐，我就很信得过。如果拉维妮娅妹妹没意见，我们很愿意试一试。谢谢您。”于是约好第二天派人来牵我。
第二天早晨，来了一位干练的年轻人。他先挺高兴，看到我的膝盖，便失望地说：“先生，真没想到您会推荐一匹有伤疤的马给我家几位小姐。”
“漂不漂亮，得看做得怎么样。”我主人说，“你只是带它去试一试。年轻人，我知道你会公平待它。要是你赶车时它不够稳当，就送它回来。”
我被领到新家，进了舒适的马厩，吃过草料，自在地歇着。次日，马夫给我擦脸时说：“这跟当年黑骏马的星斑一模一样，个头儿也差不离。真不知道它如今在哪儿。”
他擦到我脖子上从前放过血的地方，摸到皮下凸起的小结，身子忽地一震，仔细端详起我来，嘴里自言自语。“额心有白星，右边有一只白蹄，小硬结又正长在这儿……”他再往我背上一看。“天哪！这儿还有那一小撮白毛，约翰管它叫‘美儿的三便士’。一定是黑骏马！美儿，你认得我吗？我是小乔·格林，差一点把你害死的那个！”他一下又一下地拍着我，高兴极了。
我不敢说我认得出他。如今他已是一个挺拔的青年，长着黑鬓须，声音也是大人的声音。可我知道他认得我，我也确信他就是乔·格林。我很欢喜，把鼻子凑过去，想告诉他咱俩是朋友。我还没见过一个人能那么高兴。
“公平地待你？那还用说！我倒要知道哪个混账跌坏了你的膝盖。老朋友，你在什么地方吃了苦啊。从今往后，要是你日子过得不舒坦，那可决不会是我的缘故。真希望约翰·曼利也能来看你。”
下午，我被套在一辆低低的游园小车上，带到门前。埃伦小姐要亲自试我，格林陪着。她车赶得好，我不一会儿就知道。她对我的步子也很满意。我听见乔在讲我的往事，说他敢断定，我就是从前戈登乡绅家的那匹黑骏马。
我们回去时，她的姐妹们出来打听我表现如何。她把刚听到的一切说了，又说：“我一定得给戈登夫人写信，告诉她心爱的马儿来了我们家。她得多么高兴！”
接下来一个星期左右，我每天都拉车出去。我看来确实稳当，拉维妮娅小姐终于也壮着胆子坐了一回小小的封闭马车。这下事情定了。她们留下我，也让我重新叫回原来的名字“黑骏马”。
到现在，我已经在这快活的地方过了整整一年。乔是个再好、再体贴不过的马夫。我的活儿轻快又愉快，力气和精神正一点点回来。前些天瑟拉古德先生跟乔说：“在你这里，它准能活到二十岁，也许还不止呢。”
威利一有机会就来跟我说话，把我当成他特别要好的朋友。家里的几位小姐答应过，绝不再把我卖掉。我没什么可怕的了。我的故事也就在这儿讲完了。那些苦日子都过去了，我到家了。常常在还没睡醒的时候，我以为自己仍在伯特威克的果园里，正和老朋友们一道，站在苹果树下。
